Brian Greene said: “as particles … try to move through space, they have to burrow through the Higgs field, and that is what gives them mass”. Does that mean that particles that keep at rest in the frame of the Higgs fied are gravitationally massless? Brian Greene’s “explanation” is one of many popularizations of physics that are intended to make difficult topics accessible to the “unwashed masses” but in reality, achieve the exact opposite. I would put it in the same basket in which I put the “rubber sheet” analogy of gravity, the “expanding balloon” description of cosmic expansion, even the “miniature solar system” models of the atom. Then I would put that basket out onto the curbside for collection. No, particles do not “burrow through” anything. If they “burrowed” through anything, that would mean a loss of kinetic energy through dissipative processes. Soon enough, everything would come to a halt, floating in some sticky molasses I suppose… But no, I swear, that is not how the Higgs works. Remember that mass is energy? No, mass is not “converted” into energy or vice versa. What we call inertial mass, or rest mass, is the internal energy-content of a thing. That’s what E = m c 2 is about, not about nuclear energy or converting anything into anything: It literally tells you that mass and (internal) energy are the same thing. Equivalent. Unsurprisingly, the equation itself is called the mass-energy equivalence relationship. In the Standard Model of particle physics, most particles start off as massless particles, but they interact with the Higgs field. However, the Higgs field has a very peculiar property. In empty space (i.e., the lowest energy state achievable, the vacuum) the Higgs field itself is not “empty”, so to speak. So particles can interact with it even when there’s supposedly nothing there. In effect, particles interact with the vacuum. Interaction means potential energy. (E.g., when two objects interact by, say, repelling one another, you need to invest energy to push them together, and that energy will be “stored” as their interaction energy while they are close to each other.) When an initially massless electron, for instance, interacts with the vacuum, it means it carries that interaction energy with it, no matter what it does or where it goes. And because the vacuum is everywhere, so to speak, the electron cannot get rid of that interaction energy. It’s always there. That interaction energy shows up, for all practical intents and purposes, as part of the energy-content of that electron. And as I stated above, energy-content means inertial mass. So the electron behaves as a massive particle, because no matter where it goes, what it does, it carries along that interaction energy with the vacuum Higgs field (to be more precise, the so-called vacuum expectation value, or v.e.v., of the Higgs field). So I stress, no “burrowing” is involved. The Higgs field has no rest frame, and how fast or how slow the particle moves with respect to this non-existent rest frame is irrelevant. In its own reference frame, a particle is always at rest. But it still has inertial mass, because the potential energy of its interaction with the Higgs field is there, no matter what.

Does the explanation of the interaction of three or more stellar objects subject to mutual gravitation require using Mandelbrot mathematics? I am assuming that this question was inspired in part by the new Netflix series, 3 Body Problem, (grumble, at the very least, they should have kept the hyphen — here, the adjective is “3-body”) their adaptation of Liu Cixin’s novel, The Three-Body Problem. In the novel, of course, we learn that planetary orbits in a ternary star system are chaotic and inherently unpredictable, an unsolvable mathematical problem. Almost none of that is true, actually. (But don’t let that ruin your enjoyment of the story. I have not yet seen the new series, but I read the books, which are excellent, and saw the Chinese television adaptation, which was better than decent.) In the actual, physical universe in which we live, system of three, four, or seven hundred billion bodies are all governed by the same set of (conceptually simple) second-order differential equations. However, the nature of these systems is that the mathematical solutions are sensitive to the initial conditions; even a small perturbation can, over time, cause large-scale changes in the solution (the famous “butterfly effect”). This makes systems of three or more bodies different from two-body systems that are characterized by stable solutions (in which the error in initial conditions accumulates linearly, does not “blow up” uncontrollably.) But the emphasis is on “over time”. We are talking astronomical timescales! Give me a planet in a 3-body system with its position along with the positions of its host stars measured with reasonable (say, late 19-th century photographic) accuracy over the course of a few weeks or months, maybe a few years (depending on the size and characteristic orbital periods of the system), and chances are, I can reliably predict its orbit for the next several million years. Seriously. And it’s not even very hard; I can write a piece of code, an integrator with the requisite accuracy, even half asleep, though I admit I may have to cheat and look up a few formulas that I do not remember off the top of my head. So no, no fancy mathematics is needed. Systems of differential equations with unstable solutions are present everywhere. We know how to deal with them. There are no miracles: Noisy data means noisy solutions, but when it comes to astronomy, the observations tend to be very accurate even when done with 19th century methods and equipment. How is the speed of gravity determined? First of all, while I recognize that this is a bit of semantics, there is no “speed of gravity” any more than there is a “speed of electromagnetism”. Gravity is an interaction, it does not have an inherent speed. However, influences in the gravitational field, far from sources, travel as transverse waves, and these indeed do have a speed. Theory tells us that this speed is the same as the speed of influences in the electromagnetic field, i.e., electromagnetic waves such as light. While few had real doubts that this prediction is valid, its first observational test came seven years ago with the LIGO event GW170817. This gravitational wave event turned out to be the collision and merger of a pair of neutron stars, an event that was also detectable in a multitude of electromagnetic frequencies. The electromagnetic and gravitational signals arrived at the same time, even though they event took place some 130 million light years from here. This tells us that indeed, gravitational and electromagnetic waves traveled at the same speed. As a matter of fact, this had a direct impact on theory. There are proposed alternative theories of gravitation in which there is not one but two (or more) metrical fields, one determining the speed of gravitational waves, the other, the speed of electromagnetic waves. These “bimetric” theories were essentially falsified by the GW170817 observation.

How can virtual particles become real particles e.g. while Hawking radiation? I suspect that this question was at least inspired by the popular, but fundamentally misleading “explanation” that Hawking radiation is about the creation of virtual particle-antiparticle pairs near the horizon, one of which is swallowed by the horizon, while the other is released as a “real” particle. This explanation, though it first appeared I believe in Hawking’s own popular science book, is nonetheless nonsensical, in direct contradiction with Hawking’s own 1974 paper (Nature 248 (5443)), which explains how gravitational vacuum polarization, along with the past-future asymmetry of a system in a perpetual state of collapse, leads to a net outgoing radiation. But I suspect there is also a misunderstanding here concerning the nature of particles, be they real or virtual, in the context of quantum field theory. Take the electromagnetic field. The classical theory is Maxwell’s: it’s a field theory, which is to say, it describes something that is present everywhere, with a continuously varying value from point to point in space and time. This field may be sourced by electric charges. If charges are absent, the field equations can still have nonzero solutions, which are in the form of plane waves traveling at constant velocity (the velocity that we know as the vacuum speed of light). When it comes to the quantum theory, we start with decomposing the field into elementary frequencies, kind of like how a sound can be decomposed into elementary pure sounds of different pitch. Each of these pure waves can be treated as a “harmonic oscillator”, which, in the quantum theory, has discrete levels of energy. It is these discrete levels, or packets, of energy that will be the field quanta, and it is these quanta that we perceive, under the right circumstances, as particles. When we write down the equations of fields, especially interacting fields, the equations include nasty summations (integrals) of ever more complicated interactions. As a mental aid, however, we can think of these interactions in terms of one unit, one quantum at a time, and even use neat little diagrams (the Feynman diagrams) as a bookkeeping device, keeping track of these terms. The arrows in that Feynman diagram are suggestive of particle-like behavior. Even though no actual particles are involved, it can sometimes be helpful to intuit these interactions as exchanges of “virtual particles”. Unfortunately intuition in particle physics is a dangerous business. Helpful, yes, but do not forget for a moment that these are merely bookkeeping devices. There are no miniature cannonballs, virtual or otherwise. Only interacting fields. The “particle” aspect is entirely imaginary, existing only in our heads, as a clumsy mental aid to help our limited intuition. That’s what “virtual” really means.

When the particle is being observed, does its wave function collapse into a size less point, or a very small Gaussian packet? We don’t observe particles. We observe specific properties of particles when we measure them. In an idealized measurement, when we measure a particle position for instance, it means we ensure that the particle interacts with a classical instrument that confines the particle’s position to a specific number (an eigenvalue). Consequently its momentum is completely unconfined. In a real measurement, our measuring instrument itself is made up of particles, so it’s not a purely classical instrument. Therefore, it does not perfectly confine the particle position to a number. Interpreting the particle’s state as a probability amplitude, it indeed means that, as per our measurement, we have something like a Gaussian probability distribution characterizing the particle’s position (or whatever property it was that was being measured).

How is mass not conserved when it's literally E^2-p^2, and both quantities are conserved? The equation, m 2 = ( E / c 2 ) 2 − ( p / c ) 2 , or simpler yet, using units such that c = 1 , m 2 = E 2 − p 2 , indeed describes the invariant rest mass of an isolated particle. However, it does not imply that rest mass is conserved in interactions. As a simple example, consider the collision of an electron and a positron. In the center-of-mass reference frame, their three-dimensional momenta are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction: p e = − p p where I used p to represent the 3-dimensional momentum vector. And of course both the electron and the positron have the same invariant rest mass m e . So before the collision, we have m 2 e = E 2 e − p 2 e , m 2 e = E 2 p − p 2 p , for the respective particles, from which we can also conclude that E e = E p = E (i.e., I dropped the superfluous index), so the total energy of the system is 2 E . The total momentum of the system is, of course p e + p p = 0 according to the rules of vector addition, and the total rest mass 2 m e . The collision annihilates the electron-positron pair, producing (usually) two photons. Energy and momentum are conserved. That means that the momenta of the two photons must be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so their vector sum is zero. And the total energy of the two photons is 2 E . This implies that each photon has energy E with a corresponding momentum of p = E / c in magnitude, pointing in opposite directions for the two photons. The rest mass, however, is now zero. As an aside, I would like to mention two more thoughts, not directly pertinent to what I just demonstrated, but food for thought, nonetheless. First of all, this reasoning can also inform you right away why an electron-positron pair cannot annihilate into a single photon. In the center-of-mass reference frame, the net momentum must be zero, both before and after; but the energy is nonzero. If the result of the annihilation was a single photon, it would have zero momentum but nonzero energy, which is not possible. Second, now that I demonstrated that the sum of rest masses is not invariant, allow me to offer a twist of the story. Imagine this whole thing took place inside a closed box. Both before and after, the respective particles (the electron-positron pair before the annihilation, the photons after) interact with the walls of the box that keep them confined. Well, guess what: the rest mass of the total system (measured, e.g., by measuring the force that is required to accelerate the box at a certain rate) remains unchanged throughout the process. Which is just a demonstration of the rather important point: namely that the rest mass of a system is equivalent to its internal energy-content. It does not matter what form that energy is in: kinetic energy, potential energy, even the rest masses of constituent bits. The rest mass of the box is the total internal energy of the box material and everything it encloses.

What is m in f=ma, rest mass, inertial mass, variable mass, or gravitational mass? Such an old question, yet without a decent answer! The mass in F = m a refers to inertial mass. Inertia characterizes a body’s resistance to a force. You can see how when you divide this equation throughout by the mass m : a = F / m . Which is to say that given a force, a body’s resulting acceleration is proportional to that force, but inversely proportional to the body’s mass. The greater the mass, the smaller the acceleration: a body with more mass has more inertia, more resistance to motion. The term “rest mass” is synonymous with inertial mass. Consider, in fact, the title of Einstein’s famous 1905 E = m c 2 paper, which reads in English: Does the inertia of a body depend upon its energy-content? This paper establishes the equivalence of energy-content and inertia(l mass). The term “rest mass” means the same as inertial mass. It came into usage along with another term, “relativistic mass”, which combines the inertial mass of a body (which is an intrinsic property) and its kinetic energy (which is observer-dependent). Fortunately this concept is not much used anymore as it is grossly misleading and has been the source of much confusion. I am guessing that “variable mass” in the question may have referred to this relativistic mass. Gravitational mass measures how a body interacts with the gravitational field. According to the weak equivalence principle, gravitational mass and inertial mass are identical. This is what allowed Einstein to generalize his original relativity theory (now called special relativity) and extend it to become a field theory of gravitation. A theory that treats inertial and accelerating reference frames the same way (Einstein’s original objective) naturally becomes a theory of gravitation when the reference frame associated with falling in a gravitational field does not depend on the material properties of the falling object. So to sum up, the mass m in F = m a is inertial mass; it is the same as rest mass; thanks to the weak equivalence principle, it’s the same as gravitational mass; as to the concept of variable (relativistic) mass, the best advice I can offer is to forget you ever heard about such a thing. Where is the "end" of space/time within the boundaries of our observable Universe if a black hole has an event horizon? Before I answer the question, let me stress a word in the question itself: space/time. Naive visualizations of “spacetime” as something static, an image frozen in a given moment of time, will not do. Spacetime includes all of time, it’s not a snapshot of space at some specific moment of time. So where is the end of spacetime? Well… it’s more like “when”. One “end” of spacetime in the standard cosmological model is that past moment we sometimes call the “Big Bang”: the initial singularity that marks the beginning of time. The standard model cosmology describes space as infinite, without boundary, but it has a finite age. The initial singularity is not part of spacetime. To make sense of it, imagine the mathematical concept of all positive numbers. This set “ends” at zero, but zero itself is not part of it: it is not a positive number. And the set has no other end; no matter how large a number you pick, larger numbers always exist. The same thing with the other “end” of spacetime: it doesn’t have any. The standard model cosmology has an open-ended, eternal future. Black hole event horizons are different animals, but there are also some similarities. For starters, no black hole event horizon exists “now”. That is to say, any black holes forming as a result of gravitational collapse have not completed that process formation, and will not complete it in any amount of finite time as measured by observers outside. No matter how long you wait, the matter forming the black hole might change its mind (or perhaps a previously unknown physical process might kick in) and fly apart, which it can do in principle, because there is no event horizon yet. That event horizon is a forever-future moment in time, not a specific location in space. This is true even if you were unfortunate enough to fall into a black hole; the only difference is that in that case, you would reach the moment in time called the event horizon in a finite amount of time by your own reckoning, and after that, the event horizon will be a past moment in time for you, something to which you cannot return without a time machine. Is there any way, other than throwing some mass in the opposite direction, to move forward in space? To move forward in space, you don’t need to do anything. Once a body is in motion, it remains in motion unless a force acts upon it… and in space, no such forces are usually present. However, if you want to accelerate a body, things change. Acceleration means a change in the body’s momentum. But momentum is one of those quantities that are always strictly conserved. So if you change the momentum of a body, the momentum of something else, somewhere, must change by an equal but opposite amount. Reaction mass could be that something else. This is how rockets work. However, if you find something outside of your space vehicle, perhaps you can change its momentum without throwing anything away. For instance, here in the vicinity of the Earth, you might be able to interact with the Earth’s magnetic field and accelerate; in exchange, the Earth itself would accelerate in the opposite direction, but given how much more massive the Earth is compared to a spaceship, this change in the Earth’s momentum is imperceptible. It might be possible to repeat the feat on larger scales, using, e.g., the magnetic field of the Sun or even galactic magnetic fields, albeit these fields are very weak so the sheer size of whatever equipment might accomplish this miracle likely makes the concept impractical. It is also possible to make use of the momentum of something already there, e.g., sunlight. Or the momentum of something we put there ourselves, e.g., light from a powerful ground-based laser. In both cases, the spacecraft would have a lightsail that, as it interacts with (and changes the momentum of) the light it receives, imparts a momentum on the spaceship that carries it. There is also gravitational assist: When there are at least two bodies in a system (and there are certainly more than two bodies here in the solar system) it is possible to follow a trajectory that changes direction with respect to one of the bodies, but changes direction and magnitude of velocity with respect to the other. Again, momentum is conserved: the motion of the bodies involved also changes. But again, bodies such as planets in the solar system are so much heavier than a spaceship, any change in their momenta will remain imperceptible. Throughout it all, however, the common theme is that books must always remain balanced when it comes to momentum. If your spaceship accelerates in some direction, something else — propulsion mass, a planet, rays of light, whatever — must accelerate in the opposite direction. What is the propagator for a massless scalar field, and how can you compute it using C++? The propagator for a massless scalar field, which obeys the Klein-Gordon equation ∂ μ ∂ μ ϕ = 0 , can be derived from the Green’s function of this equation, ∂ μ ∂ μ G ( x − y ) = δ 4 ( x − y ) that, in momentum space, becomes − k 2 ~ G ( k ) = − 1 , hence ~ G ( k ) = 1 k 2 + i ϵ , where we introduced a small imaginary term, as usual, to avoid the singularity at k = 0. By itself, this expression is not something you would compute numerically in a language such as C++. You may be able to derive expressions of this sort in computer algebra (either general purpose CAS with specialized packages or special purpose systems). The propagator is used in combination with the vertex rules of a theory to compute cross-sections corresponding to particle interactions. That computation itself may not be trivial as it involves divergent integrals that may need to be regularized in order to obtain meaningful results for observable quantities. In short, no, unless you first use C++ to build a CAS for quantum field theory, you would not be using C++ for this type of computation. You might use a CAS to derive an expression for an observable quantity that you then import into a C++ program for numerical evaluation (perhaps as part of a larger computation) but the propagator on its own is not something you’d likely use in C++. Why does general relativity predict that the wavelength of light will be shifted due to the galaxies mass in an effect called gravitational redshift? Relativity theory predicts two things that can result in redshift: Clocks in a gravitational field tick slower than clocks in empty space. Consider a light source that produces green light at a frequency of 6 trillion cycles a second. Suppose this light source is in a strong gravitational field. You observe it and measure that indeed, the light source produces 6 trillion cycles a second according to a clock right next to it. But then you measure that light using an instrument in deep space. The light appears yellow. You measure it and it's comes in at only 5 trillion cycles per second according to a clock next to your receiver. Even though the two clocks (the one in the deep gravitational well and the one in deep space) are identical, flawless clocks they will tick at different rates. For ever 6 ticks of the clock in deep space, the clock in the gravitational field will tick only 5 times. As that clock counts to 5, the source emits 30 trillion cycles. The clock in deep space will count six times as those 30 trillion cycles arrive. Now the funny business is that the speed of that light will be measured both at the source and at the detector at 300,000 km/s. Fewer cycles means longer wavelength, then. So the same light that appears to leave the source with a wavelength of 500 nm (that is to say, 500 nanometers between emitted cycles) will be measured at 600 nm between cycles at the receiver in deep space. This is gravitational redshift. Now this example assumed that the locations are stationary. What if they aren't? If the distance between the light source and detector decreases, each subsequent cycle will arrive a little sooner as it had less distance to travel. Conversely, if the distance increases, each subsequent cycle takes a tad longer to arrive. So this, too, can change the number of cycles that are received over a unit of time. This is the Doppler frequency shift (redshift if the distance between source and detector is increasing). Perhaps you were thinking about cosmology. Relativity theory also predicts another important thing: In the cosmos, on the largest of scales, matter is not at rest. Things are either flying apart or coming together (that is to say, the matter density of the cosmos is either decreasing or increasing over time). In our cosmos, things appear to be flying apart. When things are flying apart, the distance between them increases over time. So there is a Doppler redshift. But as the density of matter decreases over time, so does its average gravity. So if light traveled for a long, long time it's coming from a distant past when the gravitational field was stronger so clocks were ticking more slowly compared to the present. So there is also a gravitational component to this cosmic redshift. The Doppler part dominates for relatively nearby galaxies; the gravitational part, for very distant stuff. To stress, I am not talking about the individual galaxy's own gravitational field that can cause a small amount of redshift; I am talking about the overall average gravitational field (i.e., the average magnitude, say, of the curvature scalar, to be a tad technical) that changes over time as the matter density of the cosmos decreases. Does matter lose mass or energy by creating gravity? Gravity creates energy in the movement of all other matter. Doesn’t this have to be conserved? The law of conservation of energy. Or do we just not understand gravity? Matter does not “create” gravity. Matter interacts with the gravitational field. Anything with energy-momentum interacts with the gravitational field. The potential energy associated with the gravitational field is usually negative. You need to invest energy when you lift something away from a gravitating body. You get that energy back when you let the thing fall. So if we take the energy between two bodies zero when they are far apart with negligible gravitational influence on one another, as they approach each other, they accelerate and energy is extracted from the gravitational field. So the field energy is negative. When astronomical bodies coalesce and form a self-gravitating structure, the negative gravitational energy is balanced by the positive kinetic energy that the bodies gain as they approach each other. Depending on how things unfold, they may remain in motion for a long time; or they may, for instance, collide, with all that kinetic energy turning into a more random form of kinetic energy, heat, which through repeat collisions of particles and the resulting acceleration, becomes electromagnetic radiation (light, heat, etc.) and is emitted into deep space. Or, if the bodies are very heavy and very compact, some of that kinetic energy might even turn into substantial quantities of gravitational radiation! That, too, can carry energy away from the system. Overall, the books remain balanced, as always. Conservation laws prevail. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

What is the cause of a black hole's immense strength? How is it possible for something to have infinite density and gravity? A black hole does not have immense strength or infinite density. Mostly, no infinite gravity either. Take a black hole that has the same mass as the Sun. Put it in place of the Sun. Guess what happens to the Earth? Apart from the lack of sunlight (which would be bad news for us humans) absolutely nothing. The gravity of that black hole is exactly the same, finite gravity as that of the Sun. Density? Sure, a stellar sized black hole is dense. Actual black holes do not form at a mass much less than about three times the mass of the Sun. But even neutron stars are insanely dense, many trillions of times denser than water. But… this may come as a surprise but very, very large black holes are not so dense at all! When we talk about the largest supermassive black holes, they can form at densities less than the density of ordinary water. It’s only when the black hole is relatively small (by that, I mean, three times the mass of the Sun, which would be “only” a million times the mass of the Earth) that such insane densities are encountered as matter collapses into a black hole. And then, the gravity. As I said, at the same distance as the Sun, a one solar mass black hole has the same gravity as the Sun. Far from infinite. So let’s get a little closer. In the case of the Sun, the closest we can get to its center is about 700,000 kilometers, before we collide with the Sun’s surface. At that distance, solar gravity is powerful (about 30 times the gravity of the Earth at sea level) but far from infinite. And you cannot get any closer, because now you would be inside the Sun. But now take that black hole. A black hole with the same mass as the Sun has an effective radius of only about 3 kilometers. Going from 700,000 to 3… as you know, gravitational acceleration is proportional to the inverse square of distance. So now we are up to trillions of times Earth gravity! And that’s just the Newtonian result. Once we take relativity theory into account, there is, after all, one infinity to deal with. At exactly the event horizon, you would literally need an infinitely powerful rocket exerting an infinite force to hover. But that’s because the event horizon has this strange spacetime geometry: “hovering” means the same thing as moving at the vacuum speed of light. Which, as we know, is not possible without an infinitely powerful rocket. But anywhere outside the event horizon, gravity is finite. And it’s strong not because the black hole’s gravity is stronger than the gravity of another object of the same mass, but simply because you can get that much closer to it. As another example, take the Earth. Its radius is roughly 6,370 kilometers or just under 4,000 miles. The radius of a black hole of the same mass? Less than 9 millimeters. Just over one third of an inch. How does Einstein's equation demonstrate the conversion of matter into energy? Can this process be reversed to create more matter than needed? It does not. The famous equation, E = m c 2 (which is not really called Einstein’s equation, but let me put pedantry aside for a moment) is absolutely NOT about any conversion of “matter” into energy. To explain what this equation IS about, first allow me to recall the title of the paper in which this equation (in a slightly modified form) is introduced: “Does the inertia of a body depend upon its energy-content?” (Ist die Trägheit eines Körpers von seinem Energiegehalt abhängig? Annalen der Physik. 18:639, 1905.) The question is answered by the paper in the affirmative, establishing something important: that what we know as the inertia, i.e., the mass (its resistance to acceleration) of a body is, in fact, its energy-content. You add energy to a body (e.g., making it warmer), its inertia increases. You remove energy from a body, its inertia decreases. Notably, the equation is not about converting anything into anything. It is, in fact, called the mass-energy equivalence relation. Which is to say, it expresses recognition of the fact that a body’s mass (its inertia, resistance to acceleration) and its intrinsic energy-content (not to be confused with energy that exists relative to other reference frames, such as the body’s kinetic energy in a moving observer’s reference frame) are really equivalent: they are the same thing. Now about that pedantry bit: The expression, “Einstein’s equation”, is usually used to refer to the equation R μ ν − 1 2 g μ ν R = 8 π G T μ ν , which is Einstein’s (field) equation for gravitation, i.e., the fundamental equation of general relativity. Note that all along, I’ve been silent about the word “matter”. This concept is not even defined in relativity theory. The contribution of matter to the field equations is characterized by the stress-energy-momentum tensor T μ ν , but the theory remains silent about what “matter” really is. This is also true when it comes to E = m c 2 . Presumably a “body” would be made of “matter”, but again, the theory remains silent as to its nature. It only talks about its specific, measurable properties, namely its resistance to acceleration (mass) and changes in its energy-content. The closest thing to “creating” matter happens in particle accelerator experiments, when lighter particles collide with plenty of excess kinetic energy as measured in the reference frame of their common center-of-mass. The collision converts them into new particles, which may be heavier than the progenitors, which is to say that some of that kinetic energy of the collision now becomes the internal energy-content of the collision products. These products are usually short-lived, unstable particles however, so very quickly they decay back into lighter particles, with some (most?) of their energy-content now turning back into the kinetic energy of these decay products. But other than the fact that all along the process, mass-energy is conserved, the equation E = m c 2 has nothing to do with such processes of particle creation and annihilation. How is the speed of light considered constant in all frames despite the effects of gravitational and inertial time dilation? Distinguish between local measurements vs. measurements made from a distance. Suppose a photon zings by and you measure its speed: It’s 299,792,458 m/s. Other observers, at the same place where you are and at the same time, measuring the same photon, will measure the same speed even if those other observers are moving relative to you. However, when you look at distant photons, the situation changes. What you observe is subject to relativistic effects such as length contraction and time dilation. The speed you deduce can be anything. If you are on the surface of a neutron star and measure events far from that neutron star, you’ll see things unfold rapidly, as if you viewed them in fast forward mode. Conversely, if you are floating in deep space and check what happens on the surface of that neutron star, things will appear painfully slow, including photons. But even in these cases, as you look at those distant locations, if there are observers there with clocks and meter sticks, you will be able to verify that according to those clocks and meter sticks, co-located with the photon, light still travels at 299,792,458 m/s, always, so long as it’s a vacuum outside. How likely is it that antigravity is possible? What are some possible ways that anti-gravity could exist, if any? Well, in a sense it does exist, but not necessarily in a form anyone might consider useful. You may have heard of dark energy, driving the accelerating expansion of the universe. Why accelerating? Normally, gravity would slow down the expansion, perhaps even reverse it, since it is pulling things together. However, there’s a subtle but important point when we switch over from Newtonian gravity to general relativity. In Newtonian gravity, the source of gravitation is mass density. This is formally written in the form of Poisson’s equation as ∇ 2 U = 4 π G ρ where U is the gravitational potential and ρ is the mass density. In general relativity, however, that ρ is replaced with ρ + 3 p / c 2 , where p is the pressure. (As for the rest of the symbols, G is the gravitational constant, c is the vacuum speed of light, and ∇ in this case is the gradient operator.) Normal matter has pressure, but after divided by the square of the speed of light, that pressure turns out to be negligible compared to mass density. But dark energy! Dark energy not only has pressure, but it is a) negative, b) huge. How huge? For dark energy, p = − c 2 ρ . Put that into Poisson’s equation and there you have it: For dark energy, ∇ 2 U = − 8 π G ρ . Repulsive gravity. Stuff in regions of space dominated by dark energy are pushing away from each other, accelerating cosmic expansion. As I said, not very useful unless you are into universe-building. But there you have it, antigravity, an essential feature of our cosmos if our standard cosmological model can be believed. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Does Victor Toth agree that his explanation of the cosmic microwave background with the help of pops on the square is more suitable for "substantiating" the Olbers paradox? A strange question but certainly not a silly one! First, a reminder. I used the “pops on the square” analogy to explain why light from a single instance of time (the moment of time confusingly called the “surface of last scattering” when the cosmic microwave background originated) is seen as continuous radiation. To recap: You are in a very, very, very large square, full of people as far as the eye can see and beyond. Something happens, say, a flash in the sky, and simultaneously, everyone claps once. But that is not what you hear. The moment it occurs, you hear clapping nearby. A second later, you hear the clapping from people roughly 1000 feet away beause sound travels at a finite speed. Sure, the sound diminishes with distance but there are also more people along a circle of 1000 feet in radius than nearby, so the total intensity doesn’t really diminish that much. At two seconds, you hear clapping from even more people at 2000 feet away. At 10 seconds, it’s the folks at 10,000 feet. And so on. If the square is infinitely large, the clapping never stops. This is why we continue seeing cosmic background radiation. Granted, it’s faster, but Just like sound, light also travels at a finite speed. Today, we see light (well, microwave radiation) from volumes of gas at 13.8 billion light years (light travel distance); tomorrow, we’ll see it from volumes of gas situated at 13.8 billion light years and one light day away. How does this relate to Olbers’s Paradox? The 19th century German astronomer Olbers asked a simple question: If space is infinite, and there are stars everywhere, no matter which direction we look in the sky, eventually that direction should terminate on the surface of some distant star. So why is the night sky dark? The answer, of course, is that we do not live in an eternal universe. The universe has a finite age. No matter what direction we look, eventually we run out of stars: the oldest star cannot be older than the universe itself, so beyond 13.8 billion light years, there are no more stars. Given the density of stars in the universe, that means that in most sky directions, we don’t see any stars at all. There is more to the story of course because in an expanding universe, distant stars are also dimmer as they are receding from us, but we don’t even need expansion to understand the key argument: Olbers’s paradox works only in an eternal universe. Back to my example of the clapping crowd in the square: It’s different. The folks in the crowd are not clapping continuously. The clapping is a single event. But you know what? Let’s assume a square in which folks are clapping continuously, and have always been clapping. That means that at any moment in time, you hear clapping from all of them. Nearby claps that happen now; distant claps that happened seconds, minutes, hours earlier, with the sound only reaching your ear now. If the square is truly infinite, that means that at any given moment in time, you are subjected to noise from an infinite number of people. There, Olbers’s paradox. But wait… people. People don’t live forever. Say, everyone in this imaginary square is exactly 20 years old. They have been clapping all their lives, since they were born. So that means that you hear clapping from as far away as, well, over 600 billion feet, so this is truly not realistic of course, just a thought experiment, but the point is, you get a lot of clapping, but no clapping sound reaches your ears from beyond 600 billion feet, give or take. Why? Because there were no people alive, doing any clapping in this square, more than 20 years ago! From places in the square more distant than 600 billion feet, the earliest clapping sounds have not had a chance to reach you just that! Okay, I know, I am stretching an already weird, silly analogy but still. I hope it answers the question, any possible relationship between Olbers’s paradox (which explains why the night sky is not as bright as the Sun) vs. the cosmic microwave background (which shines from all sky directions and never stops.) Is there a semantic difference between the redshift caused by gravity wells and the redshift caused by the expansion of space? First of all, allow me to take exception at the (granted, commonly used) expression, “expansion of space”. Space is not a thing. More specifically, it does not have any little markers attached to it by which its expansion, if any, could even be measured! No, it is things (galaxies, gas, dust, etc.) that are flying apart. It is the density of matter that decreases over time. And it is the gravitational field that changes as a result: a physical field that, however, can also be interpreted as the metric of spacetime. It is when folks take this interpretation a little too literally and a little too dogmatically that we end up with “expansion of space”. So then, putting these qualms aside… redshift happens as a result of the relationship between the world lines of the transmitter and the receiver. If the distance (the actual distance, which may be measurable by means of exchanging light signals, for instance) between the transmitter and the receiver changes over time, there is a velocity-induced Doppler frequency shift. If clocks at the different locations (or times!) tick at different rates, there is a gravity-induced redshift (gravity manifests itself primarily in the form of time dilation in general relativity, i.e., the rates at which clocks tick relative to one another.) It is time dilation that yields an observed redshift for light coming from a gravitational well, and it is predominantly time dilation when it comes to the redshift of “high-z” objects, that is, objects very far from here with substantial redshifts. There are some qualitative differences: when it comes to a gravitational well, we’re basically looking at a static configuration, and simply the fact that clocks deep inside that gravitational well tick slower, right now, than clocks elsewhere. When it comes to cosmological redshift, what we see is that in the distant past, matter was much denser, consequently the average gravitational potential was greater and clocks were ticking more slowly back then than they tick today. So truly, it’s gravitational redshift in both cases, just two distinct scenarios: One is the gravitational redshift due to a compact object’s gravitational field here and now, the other is gravitational redshift due to the average gravitational field characterizing the cosmos in the distant past. But fundamentally, it’s gravity in both cases. A consequence of Einstein’s field equations that connect, no, not the “geometry of spacetime” but rather, the tensor field of gravitation with the stress-energy-momentum of matter. It’s due to the weak equivalence principle that we can interpret the tensor field of gravitation as geometry, but as I stressed in many of my answers in the past, Einstein himself cautioned against taking this interpretation too literally. Otherwise it becomes an obstacle, preventing us from thinking about alternate theories of gravity that may not obey the weak equivalence principle, or quantizing gravity as a force. Einstein himself never stopped referring to gravity as a force, the utility of the geometric interpretation notwithstanding. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Is Newton's conception of gravity as incompatible with Einstein's concept of gravity, as Einstein's is from the quantum? How, or how not? None of the above incompatibilities are true. First, Newton himself knew that his gravitational theory is incomplete. It involved “action at a distance” between celestial bodies, with no means, no medium to mediate that interaction. To quote the man himself (letter to Bentley, Feb 25, 1692/93): "That gravity should be innate inherent & {essential} to matter so that one body may act upon another at a distance through a vacuum without the mediation of any thing else by & through which their action or force {may} be conveyed from one to another is to me so great an absurdity that I beleive no man who has in philosophical matters any competent faculty of thinking can ever fall into it. Gravity must be caused by an agent {acting} consta{ntl}y according to certain laws, but whether this agent be material or immaterial is a question I have left to the consideration of my readers." Einstein completed this theory, though by no means was he the first to try. In the wake of the success of Maxwell’s theory, especially after special relativity made it clear that the electromagnetic field is a fundamental entity, not just waves of some medium (the luminiferous aether), many sought a similar field theory of gravitation. It took a while to understand why a scalar theory would not work, and why a tensor theory necessarily doubles as the observed geometry of spacetime. Einstein succeeded, and by doing so, ultimately answered the riddle posed by Newton more than two centuries earlier. And of course Einstein’s theory yields precisely Newton’s in the weak field, nonrelativistic limit. General relativity is a classical field theory. It is not fundamentally incompatible with quantum physics. We can do quantum field theory on the curved background of general relativity. (Indeed, popular topics such as Hawking radiation arise precisely as a result of such an approach). We can even have quantum matter act as the source of classical gravitation, in the form of semiclassical gravity. We find this unsatisfactory, however, in much the same way Newton was not satisfied with his own theory of gravitation: We sense that it is not the final word on the subject and further improvements are needed. But we would expect such an improved theory to yield Einstein’s in the semiclassical limit, and yield Newton’s in the semiclassical, nonrelativistic limit. No incompatibilities there, just gradual improvements in our understanding, one step at a time. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Is it sexist that women are not being selected to win a Nobel Prize? Could it be that the work of those women do not measure to the actual work the winners of the awards have accomplished? Here's a quote from a recent video by Sabine Hossenfelder: [...] I wasn’t offered a job because I’m a woman. I'm not guessing that that’s what happened, I know, because they told me. You see, the guy who was head of the institute told me that, since I'm female I should apply for a scholarship that was exclusively for women in the natural sciences. Because then the institute wouldn't have to pay for me. I met Sabine (at the Perimeter Institute). My impression was that she radiated self-confident knowledge and competence. To the extent I am qualified to judge, she came across as a very sensible, good physicist with a well-earned reputation, who has put a lot on the table in her career as a professional physicist, and who would never pull the “gender card” to complain. The situation she describes sounds awfully familiar, probably repeated far too often at universities and research institutes around the world, even today. Women face a multitude of obstacles, starting with the cultural: the “hard” sciences are often presented as male pursuits, whereas women should supposedly be more interested in, I don’t know, arts, crafts, or raising babies. I suspect that this already discourages far too many talented young women. Then there is human biology: the birth of a child can burden any parent, but the burden is obviously disproportionately the mother’s, starting with pregnancy and childbirth itself. Family expectations may pile on top of cultural stereotypes: The young mother may be expected to stay at home with the children, while the father assumes the traditional role of breadwinner. Obstacles like that which Sabine encountered may not even be based on downright gender prejudice. Institutions may simply be worried that hiring a woman is like playing the lottery: The woman may get pregnant, perhaps multiple times, absent from her position for extended periods of time. But yes, old-fashioned, ugly gender prejudice is likely still present at times, not to mention unacceptable behavior like harassment or worse. I recall a discussion I once had with someone, about Sabine: the person I was conversing with questioned her competence, unfavorably comparing her to a much younger (male, of course) physicist who has not yet published anything notable at the time. It was clear to me that I was witnessing an outburst of classic, old-fashioned sexism. And it doesn’t take much to change the statistic. When you look at Nobel laureates, they represent an extreme, one of the trailing ends of the Gaussian curve characterizing the scientific community. All it takes is a small shift of the curve to the left, barely noticeable in its central part, for there to be an order-of-magnitude difference near the trailing ends. In short, even if I boldly assume that we no longer need to worry about gender bias in the Nobel selection process that may have deprived the likes of Lise Meitner, Emmy Noether, Cecilia Payne, Jocelyn Bell Burnell, Vera Rubin or Chien-Shiung Wu, just to name a few examples (if the names are unfamiliar, look them up, it’s worth your time), of well-deserved recognition, the cards are still far too often stacked against women by both biology and society. Writing this reminded me of one of my heroes, a person who surely would have deserved a Nobel prize, if only computer scientists qualified for one. I am of course talking about the amazing Grace Hopper, mathematician, computer scientist, and rear admiral of the United States Navy, at the time of her retirement the oldest serving commissioned officer in the armed forces of the United States. One of the things she is known for may not be universally liked but it is still widely in use today, nearly 65 years after its invention: The COBOL programming language.

Can a massless photon be depicted with kinetic energy since kinetic energy involves mass, yet a photon is massless which diametrically discredits Planck's and Einstein's disjointed theories? Kinetic energy does not necessarily involve mass. For particles that have nonzero rest mass, the expression for kinetic includes their mass. But kinetic energy is a much more general concept, a constant of the motion if you wish, applicable to all systems that are governed by equations that are time translation invariant. And yes, that includes massless photons. In the “disjointed” theory of relativity, of course, time is an observer-dependent concept. Invariance under spacetime translations, however, implies the conservation of a four-dimensional quantity, the so-called four-momentum of the object. Once a specific coordinate system is picked, this four-momentum can be split into an energy term and a three-dimensional conventional momentum term. But this split is, again, observer-dependent. For objects with rest mass, there exists a reference frame in which the object is, well, at rest. In this reference frame, obviously there is no kinetic energy. There is still an energy term, however; it’s the rest mass-energy of the object. In all other reference frames, the energy term is the sum of the rest mass-energy and the kinetic energy of the object. If the object is massless, however, it has no rest mass and no rest frame; the energy term is entirely due to kinetic energy in all reference frames. Why were the breakthroughs in the development of physics from 1900 to 1935 far greater than subsequent period? It seems that those 35 years were the period of the greatest explosion in the development of physics in the entire science history. Is the premise of this question really valid? Permit me to challenge it. Certainly, the first one third of the 20th century saw not one but two extraordinary revolutions in physics, the development of relativity theory and that of the quantum theory. But similar, profound revolutions have taken place previously. Perhaps the biggest, I’d argue, something even more profound than the development of quantum physics and relativity, was the shift from the Aristotelian to the modern view of the physical world. In Aristotle’s view, the celestial spheres and the terrestrial sphere were governed by different laws. In the celestial spheres, motion was eternal. In the terrestrial sphere, motion was temporary, always coming to an end without a mover of some sort. The celestial spheres were “perfect”, unchanging, whereas the terrestrial sphere was subject to decay. With the work of Copernicus, Kepler, Galileo, and ultimately, Newton, this was replaced by a world view in which the same fundamental laws governed heaven and earth. And these fundamental laws became precise, expressed using the language of mathematics, in particular the mathematics of infinitesimal changes, i.e., calculus. I cannot stress how fundamental this shift was to the development of modern science. Compared to this, the birth of quantum physics and the theory of relativity are… well, almost child’s play. Moving on, in the late 18th and the 19th century, another groundbreaking development took place: the advent of the “action principle”, the idea that the equations that govern a physical system can be derived by minimizing the “action”, a mathematical expression that characterizes a system’s evolution over time. It is difficult to stress just how critical the action principle has become in nearly all branches of fundamental physics: It governs mechanical systems, both particles and continua; classical field theories (electromagnetism and gravitation); and it forms an absolutely crucial foundation for the quantum theory. And no, physics did not come to an end in the 1930s. What was yet to happen was the development of quantum field theory, including non-Abelian theories, the modern understanding of the role intrinsic symmetries play in the behavior of quantum fields, ultimately leading to the development of the Standard Model of particle physics, a model that (as far as we know) accurately describes all the fundamental building blocks of the universe excluding gravitation. So yes, the first third of the 20th century was a remarkable period in physics, when two major revolutions took place at the same time. But that does not mean that similar, profound shifts in our understanding have not taken place before or after. And not just in physics; how about, for instance, biology, the understanding of DNA and the molecular foundations of genetics, that took place in the 1950s? It is perhaps true that fundamental physics has been a bit “stuck” in the past 50 years, not so much for lack of ideas but for lack of experimental evidence: Without hints from Nature, we can’t tell which approach, e.g., makes better sense as we try to improve the compatibility of the quantum theory and gravitation. Even so, look at the application side of things. It wasn’t that long ago that things like a blue LED seemed like unachievable “holy grails” in semiconductor technology, yet here we are, chances are you are reading this on a device with an OLED display, sitting in a room lit by a high power white LED lightbulb. Or not. Maybe you are not reading my silly words at all, consulting instead with a large language model, a culmination of some 70 years of research that began with simple “neural networks” designed to simulate the basic structure of neurons in the animal brain? So breakthroughs happen all the time. The first 30-odd years of the 20th century must have been an amazing time to be alive for a physicist, but you know what, I much rather do physics in 2024, with all the knowledge we have since added in the intervening century. Isn’t it true that the general theory of relativity suggests the existence of black holes, white holes, negative value e=mc2 energy, wormholes, quantum entanglement, cosmological, constant gravitational waves, and a host of other amazing things? No. General relativity does not “suggest” any of the above. General relativity provides one thing: a set of equations that govern the behavior of the gravitational field. That’s it. End of story. R μ ν − 1 2 R g μ ν = 8 π G T μ ν . That is all. This equation has many solutions, just like Maxwell’s equations for the electromagnetic field have many solutions. Just because something is a solution of the field equations of a theory does not mean that this solution represents physical reality. Solutions for equations like this one are constrained by conditions. These could be “boundary conditions” (e.g., the expectation that the field vanishes large distances from a source). These could be symmetry conditions (e.g., the expectation that a compact mass has a spherical gravitational field that does not depend on time.) These expectations narrow down the range of solutions. So let’s pick apart the specific points listed in the question. Well, I hope my answer puts those questions into a proper perspective. We can be impressed by the magnificence of Nature and be grateful for our ability in these modern times to actually make sense of some of it without turning explanations into science-fiction fairy tales. Nothing wrong with science-fiction, mind you; my favorite genre. We just need to be careful not to confuse it with reality. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

What would happen if something went through a black hole? What would happen if something went through a black hole? Well, I’d say it’d be proof that time travel exists, and perhaps the television series Dr. Who is not a science-fiction show but a documentary. You see, the event horizon of a black hole is not something that is here, now, which you can go “through”. The event horizon of a black hole is a moment in time. In fact, so long as you are outside of that event horizon, it forever remains a future moment in time. And if you reach the horizon to get “inside” the black hole, the horizon becomes a past moment in time for you. So to go “through” a black hole (which is to say, enter the black hole and then re-emerge, in the finite future of any outside observer), you’d have to travel backwards in time. Kind of hard to do without a time machine like the aforementioned Dr. Who’s fames TARDIS.

If gravity is a warping of space-time, why is it that we see no distortions in our visual field? Well, the main reason is that Newtonian gravity is primarily about distortions of time, that is to say, the rate at which clocks tick. The stronger the gravitational field, the slower clocks tick in it compared to other clocks situated elsewhere. Compared to this temporal distortion, spatial distortion is exceedingly tiny. As a matter of fact, the temporal distortion is tiny, too. Here on the surface of the Earth, terrestrial gravity alters the rate of clocks by roughly one part in a billion compared to clocks in deep space. It would take several decades before the difference between two such clocks reaches one second. Yet the distortions are visible, just not with the naked eye. In 1919, an expedition lead by Arthur Eddington was measuring just that: the visual distortion due to the Sun’s gravity during a total solar eclipse. For a long-duration moon mission, would an Earth-corrected time standard be required, or would periodic corrections to Earth time be sufficient? It depends on what you want to achieve. As others noted, gravitational time dilation amounts to a roughly 60 microsecond difference per day. If you are only interested in making sure that you don’t miss your favorite TV show, you have nothing to worry about for at least a good half century, which is when the cumulative difference reaches about a second. But as they say, the devil is in the details[1]. What are you using your clocks for? If you are doing navigation using precise radio signals, GPS-like, then keep in mind that every microsecond amounts to about 300 meters when it comes to straightforward length measurements; depending on the geometry of the problem, when you are looking at satellites at an angle, the navigational errors can quickly add up to several kilometers. Needless to say, when you’re landing a spacecraft, several kilometers might mean the difference between a nice, flat region vs. the boulder-filled interior of a nasty lunar crater. Not good! Moreover, while it is true that the time dilation averages to about 60 microseconds a day, it is highly variable. The rate at which clocks tick on the Moon relative to terrestrial clocks (or clocks in intermediate orbits around the Earth, like GPS clocks) depends on many factors other than lunar gravity, including the gravity of the Earth itself, the gravitational field of the Sun (the Moon may be closer to, or farther from the Sun than the Earth at various points during a lunar orbit, and this affects relative clock rates) not to mention the relative motion of the respective clocks. Ultimately it is still a simple problem (just account for all the sources of gravitational time dilation and add them all up — nonlinear effects can likely be safely ignored as they are many orders of magnitude smaller) but it still requires making sure that everything is properly accounted for at the requisite level of accuracy. Long story short, my expectation is that before long, there will be a lunar reference time standard, likely as a result of some international agreement. Future missions, including missions that might be used to assist navigation in cislunar space, will probably use that standard. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Can I buy a quantum computer? Are they real, or are they just news wanting views? Well, yes… but no. Allow me to explain. Or rather, allow me to begin my answer with a question: What do we call a “quantum computer”? Because the definitions, unfortunately, shift depending on who is offering the announcement of the day about yet another breakthrough, yet another declaration of “quantum supremacy”, or let’s face it, yet another request for research grants. So if money is no object, what can you buy that others might call a “quantum computer”? Well, you can certainly buy an experimental device that has a couple of qubits (the basic unit characterizing the capabilities of a quantum computer). You may get one for a few thousand dollars. Not very useful or practical, mind you, just an educational toy. If you have a lot more money, you can also buy a system (or more likely, have one custom-built for you) with more qubits, but apart from the sticker shock, be prepared for the need to set up a special facility to host, and support, the hardware. And in the end it, too, would amount to little more than an expensive educational toy, with no practical utility whatsoever. Or you can buy a system like D-wave’s quantum annealer, which is basically an analog computer that is particularly suitable for certain classes of optimization problems. But it is not a general purpose quantum computer. Which leads me to the answer I’d like to offer to my own question: a true, general purpose quantum computer is a scalable quantum computing machine. One that has as many qubits as I need, one that can be expanded with more qubits if necessary. This is not something that you can buy no matter how much dough you have, because it is not something that exists today, and may never exist in the future. Some compare the current state of quantum computing to the dawn of digital computers. But that is a false comparison. Sure, the Intel 4004 CPU was very primitive compared to its present-day counterparts. But the architecture was scalable. I could, in principle, build a circuit with a thousand 4004 CPUs. I could use bank switching and attach gigabytes of memory to a single 4004 CPU. Sure it would be damn inconvenient, cumbersome and very costly, but the system would work. There is no underlying physics principle that prohibits the existence of a million-CPU supercomputer with a terabyte of RAM, based on the 4004. It would be a darn stupid thing to build, but it can exist. This is not the case with quantum computing. You cannot add qubits galore, no matter how much money you have. The culprit is fundamental physics: the famous threshold theorem, in particular. The promise of general-purpose quantum computing is based on this theorem. You see, quantum computers are based on the premise that even though qubits have only two states when they are read, during the operation of the quantum computer it’s not those two states but their superposition, characterized by a continuous quantity (e.g., the phase of the wavefunction), that interacts with similar qubits in the system. The problem is that the qubits are not only entangled with each other, they also tend to get entangled with everything else in the universe. We try to keep the qubits as isolated from the environment as possible, to prevent environmental decoherence. This isolation is necessarily imperfect. But here is where the threshold theorem kicks in: If we can keep this decoherence below a certain threshold, there exist error correction algorithms that allow a system of qubits to emulate a perfect quantum computer with fewer qubits. The trouble is, this threshold has so far proven elusive. All those machines that I mentioned above, including cheaper commercially available units or pricier research installations? None of them are scalable. None of them beat the threshold theorem. Can the theorem be beaten? An entire industry, billions of dollars are wagered on that possibility. I am in a skeptical minority: I think it will prove to be a no-go theorem. Of course it is very possible that I am wrong. But until I see a credible announcement of a quantum computer architecture that beats the threshold theorem, my skepticism remains. So then, the answer to your question is that, well, yes, you can buy systems that are called “quantum computers” and they are not deceptive, you just need to know exactly what it is that they are selling. But no, you cannot buy a true, scalable general-purpose quantum computer because no such thing exists today.

Is a single electron considered an actual particle in quantum mechanics, or is it always just a wave packet with definite properties at any given time? Oh, in quantum mechanics, a particle like an electron is always a particle, an actual, immutable particle. The waves (which is to say, the wavefunction) determine the physical properties, including the position and momentum of this particle. In the Copenhagen interpretation, this wavefunction is interpreted as a probability amplitude, and it is used in conjunction with the concept of an idealized, classical measurement apparatus, to compute the probability of finding the electron somewhere, or moving with some momentum. In quantum field theory, there are no particles, only fields. The fields are quantum fields, which is to say, just like the position of that poor electron in quantum mechanics, the field does not have definite values at specific places and times; rather, a wavefunction determines (at least in the Copenhagen interpretation) the probability of finding the field with specific values at specific places and times. However, another property of these quantum fields is that when they interact, their values go up or down one unit at a time. It is these unit excitations that we observe, in localized interactions, with particle-like behavior. So to sum up/reiterate, in quantum field theory, an electron is an excitation of the corresponding fermionic field (the electron field). The wavefunction (not to be confused with the field proper) may be interpreted as a probability amplitude that tells us the probabilities of finding the field in a definite state using a classical instrument. Interactions between fields create and destroy excitations (“particles”). In contrast, in quantum mechanics particles are eternal, there are no fields, and the wavefunction can be interpreted as a probability amplitude that tells us the probability of finding the particle in some state somewhere using a classical instrument. In quantum mechanics, is there any context where an electron has a definite position and velocity simultaneously? If such a context exists, are there known real-world situations where this is observed, or is it purely theoretical? No. A “definite” position or momentum (let’s be pedantic here and use momentum in lieu of velocity) means that both position and momentum are number-valued. That is to say, the particle is simultaneously in a “position eigenstate” and a “momentum eigenstate”. Let me explain what that means. In quantum mechanics, positions ^ q and momenta ^ p are not representable by numbers (hence the little “hat” over the symbols). They can be represented using a form of matrix algebra, or they can be represented using function operators. The fundamental statement of quantum physics is that these two things do not commute under multiplication: ^ p ^ q − ^ q ^ p = − i ℏ , where i is the imaginary unit and ℏ is the reduced Planck constant. Pretty much everything else in quantum physics follows from this commutation relation, including the famed uncertainty principle. Whether we express positions and momenta using matrices or operators, these things act upon the state of the system (which may be represented by the famous wavefunction). In the Copenhagen interpretation, we interpret this wavefunction as a probability amplitude, and use it to estimate the probability of a future experiment based on measurement results available to us at present. But measurement results are numbers, whereas ^ p and ^ q are not. Except when they are being measured! An act of measurement confines either ^ p or ^ q to an “eigenstate”, which is to say that when it acts of the wavefunction, it’s action is like multiplying the wavefunction by a number. This number is our measurement result. Now suppose that we somehow find a trick and simultaneously measure ^ p and ^ q so they are both numbers. But numbers commute under multiplication! The quantity p q − q p = 0 is always zero (notice that I dropped the hats, as p and q are supposed to be ordinary numbers now). This violates the fundamental canonical commutation relation. So either quantum mechanics is wrong, or this cannot happen: ^ p and ^ q cannot simultaneously be numbers. We know from countless experiments that quantum mechanics is not wrong, however weird it can be. Therefore, we are left with the conclusion that no, a particle cannot simultaneously be in a position and a momentum eigenstate. This was of course just a very superficial sketch of the math behind quantum physics, and, yes, it’s counterintuitive. As I stressed many times, do not expect to intuit the quantum world. It does not work that way. It’s one of those rare instances where intuition not only does not help you, it might become a formidable obstacle. Like it or not, to make sense of the quantum world, math is essential, as math is the only language that we have by which this world can be made sense of. Are frames of reference in relativity examples of charts on a manifold? Thus, are Lorentz transformations maps between charts? A chart on a manifold is a set of coordinates that covers all, or part, of a manifold. (In fact, a manifold is defined as a point set that can be covered by a finite number of finite-dimensional charts, each consisting of n-tuplets of real numbers.) A frame of reference, in turn, is associated with a specific observer. In special relativity, we can represent an inertial observer’s frame of reference with, e.g., a Cartesian coordinate chart with the observer at its spatial origin. Such a chart would cover the entirety of Minkowski spacetime. However, once we allow for accelerating observers, or worse yet, for the presence of gravitational fields, there is no longer a unique chart that we can associate with the observer. We can, however, associate with the observer a rigid frame of reference (sometimes described by the German word “vierbein” or, more generally, not restricted to four dimensions, “vielbein”) but these rigid frames are “nonholonomic”, which is to say, they do not provide a unique coordinate representation of curved spacetime in the observer’s vicinity. The (global) Lorentz transformation is a transformation between inertial coordinate systems in Minkowski spacetime. This can be generalized to curved spacetime but only as a “local” transformation with the transformation’s parameters varying from point to point.

Can you explain the Planck temperature? And at any point after the commencement of the 'Big Bang', did the temperature of the universe approach or equal the Plank temperature? Can I explain the Planck temperature? Sure. It's a natural unit of temperature that we can use if we measure everything, including temperature, in units such that c = ℏ = G = 1. Of these equalities, c = 1 amounts to measuring time and distance in compatible units (say, 1 second vs. 1 light-second); ℏ = 1 amounts to measuring energy and frequency (inverse time) or wavenumber (inverse length) in compatible units. As for G , however, G = 1 amounts to setting a "natural" unit of energy relative to which everything else can be measured. If we have a natural unit of energy, we also have a corresponding natural unit of temperature, which coincides with a system in which individual degrees of freedom are associated with this energy. How fundamental is this natural unit? No one really knows. Planck units were first proposed more than a century ago by, you guessed it, Planck, but other than offering a "natural" system of units, do they have any physical significance? Many folks believe that our best theory of nature to date, quantum field theory, is only an "effective" theory, and that at the Planck scale, the theory breaks down. Others insist that at the Planck scale, quantum effects of gravitation become important. But these are speculative conjectures, not knowledge. The Planck scale is so many orders of magnitude beyond anything we can test experimentally or through astrophysical observations, we really have no idea how things truly work on that scale. So I suppose I lied. Maybe I cannot really explain the Planck temperature after all. Or the physical significance, if any, of any of the other Planck units. Other than that they serve as a sensible "natural" set of units in which it is easier to write down our equations. Same goes for times “after the commencement of the ‘Big Bang’”. The earliest we can go back to with any reasonable certainty of knowledge is about a picosecond after the ‘Big Bang’. But this time, the universe was many orders of magnitude colder than the Planck temperature. As to what happened before, whether even that picosecond was just a picosecond or an eternity, anyone can speculate, but no one knows. The so-called Planck epoch is much too far beyond what I’d even call “informed speculation”.

Can gravity be repulsive according to general relativity? How could this concept be tested through experiments? Yes, gravity can be repulsive. In fact, repulsive gravity is the reason why, in the standard cosmological model, the expansion of the cosmos has been accelerating for the past five billion years, give or take. You may be familiar with the classical field equation for gravitation, Poisson’s equation: ∇ 2 U = 4 π G ρ , where U is the Newtonian gravitational potential, G is Newton’s constant and ρ is the mass density. (The inverse square law of gravitation follows from this expression, when \rho characterizes a compact source.) However, this equation must be modified when the medium has relativistic pressure, which is to say, when p / c 2 (with p being the pressure, c being the vacuum speed of light) is comparable in magnitude to ρ . In this case, we need to write ∇ 2 U = 4 π G ( ρ + 3 p / c 2 ) . The weirdest part is that pressure can be negative. In fact, any value between − c 2 ρ ≤ p ≤ c 2 ρ yields self-consistent physics. (When p < − c 2 ρ , the universe becomes unstable; when p > c 2 ρ , the speed of sound becomes greater than the speed of light, violating causality.) For the famous “dark energy” of standard cosmology, p = − c 2 ρ . This means that for dark energy, Poisson’s equation actually becomes ∇ 2 U = − 8 π G ρ D E . Note the change of sign.
