At 0 Kelvin, the motion of particles is completely halted. But is there a phase, under some circumstances, where the subatomic particles (electrons) also stop moving? Sigh. You received many answers to this years-old question, but several of them seem united in terms of a key misunderstanding: "particles" are not miniature cannonballs and the classic concept of "motion" does not apply. But first of all, it's important to note that 0 K is not an achievable state. It is a consequence (or if you wish, a particular restatement) of the third law of thermodynamics. Having said that, the meaning of 0 K for a system is that it is in its unique lowest energy or ground state. It is not about motion or the absence of motion, it is about the fact that no lower energy state exists: The system can only receive energy by interacting with other systems, it can no longer transfer energy to those other systems. To elaborate further, think what thermal equilibrium means. You bring two systems into contact, energy flows from the warmer to the colder system until the two have the same temperature. At that point, the transfer of energy ceases. Now a system that is at absolute zero does not have any energy left to transfer to other systems; it can only receive energy from other systems if brought into contact with them. This statement remains valid in both classical and in quantum physics, but the meaning is different. If the world consisted of classical particles, miniature cannonballs, absolute zero would indeed mean that all motion ceases, and the system has no residual potential energy either that could bring parts of it into motion. In the case of quantum systems, the concept of "motion" may lose its meaning completely (atoms are not miniature solar systems with electrons orbiting!) but the basic concept remains the same: Absolute zero means that the system can only receive energy from other systems as it comes into equilibrium with them, it cannot release energy. Lastly, this has nothing to do with the uncertainty principle. Some characterized it as a limitation of our knowledge of particle positions and velocities. That is nonsense. As I said, particles are not miniature cannonballs. Their positions and momenta have no classical analogies. They are described mathematically by “non-commuting” entities, which is to say, their values are not at all like the ordinary number-valued positions that we are used to in the classical world. Sorry, we cannot intuit this. Math is needed. Suffice to say, it means that if one of these quantities, say, the position is momentarily number-valued, the other cannot be number-valued at the same time. The “particle” simply does not HAVE a classically meaningful position and velocity at the same time. But again, while this explains why I stressed the point that quantum particles are not miniature cannonballs, the thermodynamic principles here are equally valid in the classical and the quantum world. Quantum physics is not required to elaborate on the generic concept of a lowest energy state. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Can a proton be accelerated to a kinetic energy 10^25 Gev? Or would that destroy it? Not to mention it would require above 10 to the power of 25 W of power right? Sure it can, in principle. Keep in mind that kinetic energy is not an intrinsic property. It is observer-relative. Kinetic energy is not something a proton has; it is something you measure, when the proton moves relative to you (or, equivalently, you move relative to the proton). So hop into your relativistic spaceship, accelerate to roughly 99.99999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999949999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999875% of the vacuum speed of light, look out your window and presto: most protons you see will have a kinetic energy of roughly 10 25 GeV. The protons would be oblivious to your spaceship. They’d certainly not be ripped apart by anything. Of course you could also accelerate the proton more conventionally, e.g., by electric or magnetic fields. The technical details are a tad questionable, but as a principle, in a thought experiment, nothing prevents you from continuing to accelerate your proton for as long as you want. As to how much power it takes, why, that depends on how fast you want to do this. One GeV is about 1.6 × 10 − 10 joules, so 10 25 GeV is about 1600 terajoules. Suppose you are on a budget, so you are only able to accelerate your proton at a power of 1 watt. It would take a bit, roughly 50 million years assuming I used my calculator correctly (it is easy to get lost when there are so many different magnitudes involved), but if you could continuously accelerate your proton at that rate, it’d be up to 10 25 GeV. Why is graviton difficult to detect? Do we have any good reasons to believe it exits in the first place? The graviton is difficult to detect because gravity is very weak, which means that the probability of any particular graviton to interact with matter is very, very, very low. The late Freeman Dyson in his 2012 Poincaré Prize lecture calculated that the Sun, in addition to the humongous amount of thermal energy it emits as electromagnetic radiation (mostly light), also emits about 79 megawatts of thermal gravitational radiation. Now 79 megawatts is not a lot for a star, but it is certainly a respectable amount: For comparison, we’ve been able to reliably detect a mere 8 watts in the form of a radio signal from the Pioneer 10 spacecraft when it was roughly 80 times farther from the Earth than the Sun. So Dyson calculated what it would take to detect a single graviton event, i.e., an atomic transition caused by a captured graviton, from this radiation, using the entire Earth as a perfect graviton detector. His result: We’d see roughly one graviton every billion years. That is how weakly gravity interacts with matter. Concerning the second half of the question, no, we do not “believe” that gravitons exist. Belief is done in other places. Rather, we know that if the gravitational field is a quantum field much like electromagnetism, in the so-called perturbative limit (basically, when the field is weak) it would manifest itself in the form of discrete quanta, which we call gravitons. So detecting gravitons would confirm our suspicion that gravitation, too, is a quantum phenomenon. Conversely, if we had a firm prediction that gravitons should be detected in a given experiment, and we failed to see those gravitons, that would at the very least falsify the idea that gravity is similar a a quantum field theory to electromagnetism. (Perhaps it is still a quantum theory, but something manifestly different.) The trouble is, we can do neither. We can neither detect gravitons nor reliably exclude their existence based on observations that we can do. So we end up speculating. There are plenty of theories out there, both quantum theories of gravitation and alternatives. Some are better than others, but we really have no way to decide which is right: without experiment, without observation, we are blind, and although we are reasonably clever monkeys, at no time in the history of science were we able to figure out something like this on our own, without hints from Nature as far as I know. Is the NASA picture of the M87 black hole credible? 120 AU Schwarzschild radius at 54 million light years distance. It is credible, so long as you clearly understand what you are looking at. First of all, it is not a “NASA picture”. It is a picture produced by an international collaboration of radio astronomy observatories. The collaboration is called the “Event Horizon Telescope”, and they spent several years observing M87* to obtain a sufficient amount of data. The picture was synthesized from these observations. These radio telescopes, far apart, formed effectively a single instrument using a technique called very long baseline interferometry (VLBI). Basically, the radio telescopes received signals from the same source, and these signals were then phase coherently recombined. The recombined signal was than fitted against various source models, including models of the M87 black hole as well as alternatives. The best-fit model wins! With the help of this model, the radio astronomy data was then processed to form an image. The image depicts “light” (radio waves) generated in the vicinity of and behind the black hole, partially obscured by the black hole’s so-called photon sphere. The result is the famous synthesized image, its color chosen for purely artistic reasons. So it is an image that is a result of credible science. But no, it is not a NASA image. Nor is it an actual photograph: the image was synthesized using a very complex set of methods, processing several years’ worth of observations made by a worldwide collaboration of radio telescopes. And there is certainly plenty of room there for knowledgeable criticism of the observations, their interpretations, the models and the methods. Is it a coincidence that all particles with Higgs mass carry electric charges? Not sure if I’d call it a coincidence, nor is it, strictly speaking, true. Yes, the Higgs mechanism is responsible for the rest masses of all charged fermions (charged leptons and quarks). Why not neutrinos? Well, neutrinos need a different mechanism that yields the so-called mass mixing matrix, which is the secret behind the observed neutrino flavor oscillations. The Higgs mechanism is also responsible (albeit in a different way) for the masses of the electroweak vector bosons, but here, we have both the charged W-bosons and the neutral Z-boson. So there, there’s a particle that is massive thanks to the Higgs but has no electric charge. So perhaps a pertinent question is not so much why the Higgs prefers charged particles (since most elementary particles are charged) but why neutrinos have such weird behavior when it comes to mass. How do you manually compute sin, cos, or tan of any number? Something like sin 10, tan 13, cos 45.092? First of all, I would restrict myself to positive angles less than 45 degrees. For other angles, I’d use trigonometric identities. Next, I’d convert angles to radians. This is important. To a reasonable approximation, it amounts to dividing angles (expressed in degrees) by 57.3. This means that the largest angle in radians that I’ll be dealing with will be π / 4 or about 0.785, so well below 1. Now I can use the Taylor series for the sine: sin x ≃ x − x 3 / 6... OK, let’s give it a try. Suppose you are asking me to compute the sine of 70 degrees. But 70 is greater than 45, so I’ll be computing the sine of 20 degrees instead, which is the cosine of 70 degrees. Converting to radians by dividing with 57.3, I get 0.349. To three decimals, 0.349 − 0.349 3 / 6 will be 0.342. Since this is the cosine of 70 degrees, I can calculate the sine by taking the square root of 1 − 0.342 2 = 0.883. There are ways of calculating the square root similar to long division, so it can be done on paper… or just use trial and error. The result is 0.940. So let’s double-check with a calculator: I get 0.93969262. Bingo! Mind you, this is not a very efficient thing to do, especially if you need a lot of trigonometry. You might be better off using a slide rule or a table of trig functions. Which were the common methods used by engineers before the advent of electronic calculators back in the 1970s*. Indeed, if you were to find yourself in a post-apocalyptic wasteland with all electronics dead and rotting away, and you are tasked with rebuilding civilization one calculation at a time, you might do yourself a favor pre-calculating sines and cosines (and exponentials and logarithms and square roots and the like) and create a set of nice tables for later use. *Or later. I sometimes calculated trig functions using this approach on the four-function calculator that was a gift from my grandmother 50 years ago. If excitations in the "electron field” look to us like electrons and positrons, and excitations in the "photon field” look to us like photons, what do we perceive excitations in the "electric field" or "magnetic field" or "gravitational field" as? Does the proton have a finite lifetime? What is the evidence for that? Please respond. This question is very important to me. I want your answer? There is no observational evidence of proton decay. The only evidence that we have is that if protons do decay, their half-life is incredibly long, on the order of 10 34 years or more. In the Standard Model of particle physics, there’s no mechanism for proton decay. As a general rule a decay happens if there exists a combination of particles with less rest mass-energy than the original particle, while preserving all strictly conserved quantities such as angular momentum or electric charge. There is no known “end product” for protons that would satisfy this criteria. You might wonder if perhaps an electrically neutral, zero-spin hydrogen atom might decay into something, but the answer again is no: combining an electron and a proton yields a neutron, which has more rest mass-energy than the hydrogen atom itself. Having said that, there is a possible decay route even for protons, or rather, I should say bulk matter, but on time scales much, much longer than a mere 10 34 years: quantum tunneling through a microscopic black hole state that instantaneously evaporates in the form of Hawking thermal radiation. Does such tunneling happen? I’d be inclined to say yes, but we’ll likely never know, as it is not going to be observable by any conceivable experiment. I kind of like the idea because it is “neat” in the sense that it leads to the prediction that in the extreme far future (when the number of digits expressing number of years itself is a number so big that it requires an insane number of digits) everything, all matter evaporates into thermal radiation that, in turn, gets redshifted into nothingness by continuing cosmic expansion. But history taught us over and over again that Nature does not care what views appeal or appeal to us, so don’t take my musing too seriously. In any case, on human timescales, insofar as our experiments are concerned, the proton appears to be a stable particle, not subject to decay. What we call gravitational acceleration (9.8ms2) is a phenomenon observable only by the observer on the ground due to the dilation of time, which passes more slowly for him, giving the impression that the object in free fall is accelerating? No, that is not the way it works. At the Newtonian level, gravitational acceleration is simply a result of a force, acting at a distance between any two objects. If one of the objects is the Earth and the other is, well, anything at or near the surface of the Earth, that object will accelerate towards the center of the Earth at approximately 9.8 meters per seconds squared. In general relativity, the corresponding Newtonian potential is ascribed to the spacetime metric, specifically the “time” part of the metric that determines the rate at which clocks tick. And indeed, in a gravitational field, clocks tick more slowly than far away from the gravitating object. But this difference is minuscule. It’s barely more than one part in a billion. Tiny, tiny, tiny. So no, gravitational acceleration is not some illusion that we see because of gravitational time dilation. It is a very real deviation from straight-line, constant velocity motion. How real? Well, drop something not too heavy (we don’t want any injuries here) on your foot to find out! However, the reason why this deviation exists, why objects accelerate toward each other, is much more subtle. When we write down the relativistic equations of motion, they represent trajectories in “spacetime”. Don’t let this phrase mislead you. It’s nothing mysterious. If you draw a simple plot, with, say, time on the horizontal axis and distance on the vertical, and use it to characterize the motion of something, you drew a plot in spacetime. The thing is, the path connecting an initial state and a final state for any trajectory will have certain geometric properties in general relativity. This causes the path to be “bent”, representing a trajectory with changing velocity, i.e., acceleration. Ultimately, this bending occurs because the “length” of a trajectory is not measured in the conventional way, but in a way prescribed by the theory (Riemannian geometry, actually). The actual calculation is not terribly difficult but it cannot be explained easily as there are mathematical prerequisites for the formulas to make sense (the concept of geodesics, connection coefficients, covariant derivatives, etc.) Long story short, time dilation is minuscule (around one part in a billion) but it’s enough to change trajectories to produce a very real (not illusionary) downward acceleration (9.8 meters per seconds squared here on the surface of the Earth) by altering the trajectories of free objects. If not wearing your seatbelt was a choice instead of law, would you buckle up or go without? As a driver? Absolutely, I’d use my seatbelt. I’ve been in accidents. (Fortunately none involving personal injury to anyone). Therefore, I know both from theory and from practice what it means when the seatbelt not only keeps you safer (which you may not care about) but keeps you behind the wheel. Which means that if, after the accident, the vehicle is still (somewhat) controllable, you might regain control. You may be able to stop the vehicle before it causes additional harm to others. You may still be able to steer, preventing injury to others. All this is kind of hard to do if you have already left the vehicle through the windshield as a wingless projectile, or ended up on the rear seat as the vehicle spun about. Questions like this remind me of questions I sometimes see concerning religion: “If you are an atheist, what stops you from committing certain sins?” Here are a few words or phrases to contemplate: “Empathy”. “Compassion”. “Social responsibility”. In other words, even if you don’t care about your own safety in an accident, you could still consider that a seat belt might help you keep others, including quite possibly your own loved ones in that vehicle, safer. I know, I know, outlandish commie propaganda and all but hey, even Ayn Rand advocated enlightened self-interest: that is to say, the recognition that even if your own well-being takes precedence over that of the others, acting at least occasionally in the interests of the group might actually be beneficial to the individual…

Assuming you had a long enough cable which connects two people, would they be able to communicate if one was inside a black hole and the other outside? No, they would not, but perhaps its instructive to consider what happens from the perspective of the two participants. First, the person outside the black hole. Keep in mind that from this person’s perspective, the formation of the event horizon remains forever in the future. He would see his friend rapidly disappear from sight, but not because he’s eaten up by the black hole, not yet; rather, because as he gets really close to the black hole, any signal from him will suffer extreme time dilation and as a result, also extreme redshift. So soon enough, no matter how powerfully he transmits, and whether he does so by way of light, radio, or just yanking the cable, everything he does will appear in extreme slow motion, and the frequency (hence the energy) of any signal is redshifted down towards zero. Conversely, any signal sent by the person outside towards his friend falling into the black hole will also slow down and take longer and longer to catch up with the infalling explorer. Soon enough, we see that even signal traveling at the speed of light are too late: They will appear to slow down as viewed by the distant observer, and would simply not catch up with the infalling observer before they hit the horizon. In other words, from the perspective of the outside observer: never. As to the cable itself, what we see is that the tension on the cable increases rapidly. By the time the infalling observer reaches the horizon, the cable would be stretched infinitely, with infinite tension. That of course cannot happen, so at some point, the cable snaps. The stronger the cable, the later that happens but it is inevitable, and it will happen before the infalling observer reaches the horizon in his own reference frame. To sum up: Even though the infalling observer may reach the horizon, that moment in time remains forever in the future for the outside observer; and before that happens, the cable will snap, guaranteed, regardless how strong it is. (But if by some magic — not physics, magic — it didn’t, it’d become infinitely long and as such, unsuitable for signaling as a signal would never arrive at the other end.) Why does the weakness of gravity prevent scientists from finding the graviton? We detect particles by detecting their interactions with other particles. The strength (or weakness) of the coupling between the particles determines the “cross-section”, basically the likelihood, that a detectable interaction occurs. When the coupling is really, really weak, such interactions occur very rarely. In a 2012 lecture[1], the late Freeman Dyson presented an interesting calculation. The Sun, on account of being hot, emits not only thermal electromagnetic radiation but also thermal gravitational radiation. The same blackbody spectrum, just gravitons, not photons. Sure, gravity is very weak compared to electromagnetism, so instead of the several hundred septillion watts that it emits in the electromagnetic spectrum, the Sun “only” emits about 79 megawatts of thermal gravitational radiation, but that is still a respectable radiating power. If we had a 79 megawatt light bulb at 1 astronomical unit (the Sun-Earth distance) from here, we’d have no trouble detecting it, and no trouble detecting individual photon events from that source using a suitable detector. But this 79 megawatts is not in the form of electromagnetic waves but in the form of gravitational waves. Now Dyson imagined using the entire Earth, every last bit of it, as kind of a “perfect” graviton detector: That is, he assumed that we can somehow monitor the entire Earth in a completely noise-free setting, and detect a single atomic transition (an electron jumping to a higher orbit) as a result of capturing a graviton. I.e., direct detection of a graviton, much the same way we can detect photons with a suitable detector. The result: Dyson’s calculation told us that we would see, on average, one such graviton event every billion years or so. That is what it means to have a very weak coupling between the gravitational field and matter. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

What scientific questions need to be answered in order to tackle the understanding of dark matter? Very simple: Direct detection. The existence of dark matter is widely assumed, as we observe gravitational behavior that cannot be explained otherwise within the context of general relativity: the same general relativity that, on other scales (e.g., within the solar system) works with spectacular precision. Now of course just because something works on a size scale measured by light-hours at most does not mean that it will necessarily work equally well on a size scale measured in the thousands or tens of thousands of light-years or more. Which means that there may not be dark matter at all: perhaps the laws of gravitation must be modified! But that proves to be an immensely tricky thing to do, because most modifications run into other observational constraints. Gravitational radiation, arrival times of gravitational and non-gravitational signals from the same event, cosmological observations… the bar is set very high for such modified theories of gravity. But until we have direct confirmation of dark matter, we won’t know for sure. And so far, all we have are null results: None of the attempts to search for dark matter by nongravitational means proved successful. So the jury is still out. Were the space shuttles capable of aborting a descent from orbit and re-establishing that orbit? That might have saved the Columbia shuttle if it were possible. No, unfortunately that’s not the way it works. Let’s do a teeny bit of math. What do you think requires more energy? To lift a spacecraft to an altitude of around 400 kilometers, where the ISS orbits, or to accelerate the spacecraft to orbital speed? Well, the gravitational potential energy can be estimated crudely using E = m g h . Let’s just use g = 10  m / s 2 , and we get about 4  M J for every kilogram of spacecraft. Kinetic energy, in turn, is E = 1 2 m v 2 , and orbital speed is roughly 8  k m / s . So that would be roughly 32  M J . In other words, almost 90% of the energy spent to launch that shuttle was used to accelerate it, not to lift it. Now about that re-entry. It begins with a small burn that alters the shuttle’s orbit so that it basically intersects the upper atmosphere. The atmosphere does the rest, slowing the spacecraft down. All that kinetic energy (almost as much energy as that of a small nuclear bomb!) is converted into heat, which is why there is a need for some really serious thermal shielding. Returning from a partial descent to orbit would have required another large fuel tank like the one the shuttle used for its initial ascent. In other words, no, that is not possible. And what would have been accomplished by that anyway? The shuttle had limited consumables on board. It had to return. No, what might have saved Columbia was immediate action upon observing the foam impact during ascent. Taking the concerns seriously instead of dismissing their significance. Letting the astronauts know what they face. Authorizing impromptu repairs, even though the probability of success was low. Accelerating the preparations to launch Atlantis, while saving consumables on board Columbia as much as possible, to prolong the mission. All these options were risky of course, but they could have turned a disaster into a success, just as decades prior, the Apollo 13 disaster was turned into a spectacular, historic success by luck, clever engineering and perseverance. Then again, this is all hindsight. What if nothing had happened and Columbia survived re-entry with only minor damage? Nobody would even remember STS-107. It would be a minor footnote somewhere, something to the effect of, “STS-1xx was delayed due to extensive repairs required by Columbia after its left wing was damaged during launch of the STS-107 mission and suffered further damage upon re-entry. Launch procedures were adjusted to reduce the chances of a similar debris impact in future missions.” Sadly, that’s not what happened and seven brave souls were lost, along with a magnificent flying machine. It was eerie to watch images on CNN like the one below. As far as I can recall, these images were broadcast live (courtesy of WFAA I believe), so we CNN viewers already knew that something awful happened, even while NASA engineers were still desperately trying to reach Columbia through backup radio channels. “Columbia, Houston. UHF comm check…”

How do you know there is no speed of gravity? For the same reason I know there is no speed of water. I look at a glass of water, and it’s perfectly still. I look at a fast-flowing river, and the water is moving, well, very fast. I look the icy moon Europa of the planet Jupiter, and I see tremendous quantities of water ice moving very, very fast around Jupiter. Or maybe not moving at all if I happened to stand on Europa’s icy surface? So what exactly is the speed of water? On the other hand, I do know, for instance, the speed at which certain influences travel in water. Though it is affected by things such as temperature or salinity, sound travels roughly 1.5 kilometers a second in water. That is true in the glass of water I hold in my hands, it is true in the rivers and oceans, it is even true on Europa. So then, gravity. A static gravitational field has no speed. Why would it? Speed measures change. There is no change when the field is static. However, if you are wondering how fast changes in the gravitational field travel, far from any specific source of gravitation: Why, it’s the same speed at which changes in the electromagnetic field travel, far from any sources (electric charges). It’s called the vacuum speed of light, light being the word we associate with a particular range of frequencies of electromagnetic waves, which also include radio waves, infrared and ultraviolet light, X-rays and gamma rays. Similarly, changes in the gravitational field travel in the form of waves, and far away from sources (masses), those waves are transverse waves traveling at the same vacuum speed of light. But that is not the “speed of gravity” any more than the speed of light is the “speed of electromagnetism”. Forgive the pedantry here, but it is important to convey the correct impression: namely that speed is associated with the rate at which changes travel, the static field itself has no speed associated with it.

If a black hole never fully forms, does this mean matter is frozen, waiting to move towards the center? Does this make it possible that lower density solid matter fills its volume faster than the eh expands, given its a large black hole? That’s not exactly the way it works. A black hole never appears to fully form, as viewed by outside observers. This is due to exponentially increasing time dilation: The amount of time required for infalling particles to reach the event horizon, for the event horizon itself to form, is infinite in the reference frame of any outside observer. So as viewed by the outside observer, infalling matter indeed appears frozen. Or rather, it doesn’t appear as anything, as the same time dilation also causes extreme redshift, rendering any signal from infalling matter essentially invisible after a while. Do not try to intuit it using concepts like “lower density solid matter” or stuff like that. This is relativity theory: what we describe here is not what happens to matter, but how that matter appears to different observers. If you were to fall into a black hole (a very large black hole, large enough so that tidal effects don’t kill you) from your perspective you would a) reach the event horizon in a finite amount of time, and b) nothing particularly special happens when you do; in fact, your immediate surroundings (e.g., the interior of your spaceship) will appear perfectly normal throughout. OK, well, something special does happen but for a different reason. Suppose you descend towards the black hole. Even though the black hole has no surface and its event horizon is yet to form, you’d still see the black hole beneath your feet as a circular shadow, with optically distorted light around it, coming from distant sources. As you approach the black hole, this shadow would curl up, eventually appearing like a wall surrounding you. When it fully closes at the top, that’s the moment you cross the event horizon. At this point, from your vantage point, you’ll appear to be in a collapsing universe. In a very short amount of time, this collapsing universe will crush you, along with everything else therein, as its existence ultimately ends at the final singularity (ignoring quantum physics here which may or may not alter this outcome, and also ignoring black holes that spin or have an electric charge.) Why are black holes called black holes if they are actually white or lighter than the space around them? They are neither white nor lighter than the space around them. In classical general relativity, a black hole is truly black: it absorbs all light that hits it, and emits absolutely nothing. You really cannot get more black than that. Even with Hawking radiation, the situation is similar. Sure, black holes radiate. But astrophysical black holes have Hawking temperatures that are just a tiny, tiny fraction of the temperature of the cosmic microwave background radiation. In other words, even in this case, the black hole is a lot more black than the cosmos: it absorbs many orders of magnitude more radiation than it emits. So that’s why they are called black. Again, you really cannot get more black than these things. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Is there empirical evidence against John Moffat's modified gravity (MOG), also known as Scalar-Tensor-Vector-Gravity (STVG)? Disclaimer: I have worked with John Moffat so my views may not be impartial. The essence of Moffat’s gravity is that metrical gravity is stronger than it would be in general relativity; however, this is canceled out by a repulsive force due to a vector field interaction of finite range. For a galaxy, this means that in its inner region (where cancelation due to the vector field is present) the behavior is Newtonian; farther from the center, galaxies rotate faster because the vector repulsion is now absent and thus, gravity is stronger. The coupling parameter that governs the strength of these interactions, and the mass parameter that governs the range of the vector force are both scalar fields (perhaps the same scalar field in disguise), so the values vary from system to system. As a result, the theory can do away with the need for dark matter. Dark energy may or may not have to stay. A key feature of the theory, which distinguishes it perhaps from families of modified gravity theories that offer behavior consistent with MOND (Modified Newtonian Dynamics) is that whereas MOND-like theories are governed by a fixed acceleration scale, MOG is governed by scales determined by the mass, and distance from, the source. MOG survives many observational tests. In the solar system, treating the Sun as a single source, the parameters of the theory have negligible values so we get general relativity at the post-Newtonian level. Multimessenger observations (neutron star mergers observed using both electromagnetic and gravitational waves) are consistent with MOG as, unlike many other theories, MOG only has one metric which implies that electromagnetic and gravitational radiation propagate at the same speed. MOG is also consistent with the apparent Newtonian behavior of massive but compact galaxies, as well as the Newtonian behavior of wide binaries. And MOG may actually work well, better even than the standard cosmological model, when it comes to colliding galaxy clusters, including the famed Bullet Cluster that was supposed to be a slam dunk case in favor of standard cosmology, but also clusters that challenge the standard model. And MOG is at least approximately consistent with large-scale cosmological observations, including the large-scale distribution of matter and the cosmic microwave background (though some problems remain). Personally, I find that the biggest challenge (which can make or break the theory) is to find a consistent analytic formulation for the scalar fields’ mass dependence in the weak field limit. This has not been done yet; we have semianalytic formulas that associate values for these parameters with compact sources, but that’s the best we’ve been able to derive. Resolving this question, along with addressing the assumption that MOG, despite the presence of the vector force, satisfies the weak equivalence principle (which kind of implies that perhaps there is a metrical formulation of the theory) are issues that I consider vey important but frustratingly difficult to tackle properly.

Is the observational data that suggests that rotation curves of galaxies remains flat indefinitely a slam-dunk for MOND style theories of gravity or will traditional models ultimately prevail? In my considered opinion, not even close. Though I'd avoid using the expression "MOND style gravity". MOND (Modified Newtonian Dynamics) is just an ad hoc modification of Newton's second law designed by hand to fit rotation curves and not much else. It is not a theory of gravitation. There are proper relativistic modified theories of gravitation, which are typically not characterized by an acceleration scale (like MOND is) and which can do more than just predict-by-design the rotation curves of galaxies. Anyhow, concerning indefinitely flat rotation curves: Here is the beginning of the abstract of the paper that, I presume, triggered this question: "We use a new deprojection formula to infer the gravitational potential around isolated galaxies from weak gravitational lensing. The results imply circular velocity curves that remain flat for hundreds of kpc [...]" Note the two key phrases: "New deprojection formula" and "to infer". So the presumed rotation curves are not a result of direct observation. They are deduced from a formula that was published by the same group last year, a formula that attempts to establish a relationship between the observed surface density of a galaxy and its gravitational potential. Even if this formula is justified, using it beyond (at most) a couple of hundred kpc becomes highly questionable. For most galaxies, at that distance there is already considerable gravitational perturbation from neighboring galaxies, so it is naive to expect neat, circular orbits, determined solely by the gravitational potential of the host galaxy. In contrast, here's a plot from a paper we published with John Moffat 10 years ago, in which we use actual data from astronomers (with references cited therein), extending all the way up to (almost) 200 kpc and demonstrating that the Milky Way's rotation curve is not flat, to show how certain modified gravity theories might work, but those that predict indefinitely flat rotation curves, notably "MOND-like" theories, actually fail. In the end, of course, more direct observations will help. But I've seen plenty of rotation curves of distant galaxies that already show a noticeable decline beginning at several 10 kpc or less, to be sincerely doubtful that indefinitely flat rotation curves are a thing. Why is it so hard to believe WW2 happened for those who didn't live through it, why is WW2 so movie like in many ways? I did not live through WW2, but it is certainly not hard to believe or movie-like for me. I was born in Budapest, nearly 20 years after the war ended. Yet I grew up in a city where, especially in the smaller side streets, the scars of war were still all too readily visible. Damaged facades, bullet holes were everywhere in those old, turn-of-the-century mostly brick-and-mortar apartment buildings. (Many still have the scars in poorer, less well-maintained parts of the city or in spots not readily visible from the outside, such as internal courtyards.) And some historical buildings were still very much in ruins, such as those on historic Castle Hill on the Buda side. Another thing that was not terribly uncommon as I was growing up was the discovery of unexploded ordnance. Radio newscasts telling us that a street, an intersection was temporarily evacuated while bomb disposal teams were on scene neutralizing the threat. Still happens, by the way, though it’s much more of a rarity nowadays. More than that, my Mom lived through the siege of the city as small girl. She has many memories that she shared with me: The air raids that sent the family to the bomb shelter at Christmas, the damaged, looted apartment to which they returned many weeks later, corpses of humans and also horses, the latter sometimes surrounded by people who were carving them up for the meat. My grandmother still lived in that same apartment when I was growing up. She had a container, a large, shiny, repurposed aluminum can that she used to store flour. The can bore English-language markings courtesy of the American Red Cross, part of a post-war aid package to help a starving population. While my Mom and her family were hiding in that shelter, my father, much older, struggled to help his Jewish first wife and child and Jewish business partner with forged documents, which kept them out of the ghetto and ultimately, quite possibly kept them off the trains heading for Auschwitz. He could have been caught, carrying forged, still blank passports for instance when he was once stopped by an Arrow Cross patrol in late 1944. He was lucky: they did not search him. And of course the country I grew up in was at the time still occupied by forces of the USSR, the country that liberated the eastern half of Europe from Nazism, only to install their own version of totalitarianism in its place. So no, although (thankfully) I did not live through WW2, it is definitely not movie-like for me. People I knew, people close to me, but also places, buildings, streets all carried, sometimes still carry, tangible memories of that war.

Can particles moving backwards in time leave a black hole? Perhaps, if the following two conditions were true: These tachyons could indeed come back from the infinite future (again in the reference frame of outside observers) when the horizon forms, leaving the black hole. As far as we know, however, a) actual black holes have a finite lifespan due to Hawking-radiation, and b) tachyons do not exist (which is a Good Thing, otherwise our universe would not be causal, the future could directly impact the past.)

Dumb question of the day: If we compressed a single gram of matter to the point of creating a black hole, would it sink to the Earth's core and eventually absorb the entire planet? What would happen, how would it progress and how long would it take? Well, for starters, even if there was a known method to compress matter in such small quantities to densities far exceeding the density even in the interior of the densest neutron star, it would likely require energy far in excess of the 1 gram rest mass-energy of the matter that we started with. OK, so maybe we can start with 0.1 grams or whatever, so in the end, we create a 1 gram black hole after investing an insane amount of energy by a yet-to-be-discovered process. Well, that black hole would not last very long. It would release all its energy in 0.0000000000000000000000000465 seconds, give or take, mostly in the form of gamma radiation that would be at least ten orders of magnitude more energetic than the particle energies in the Large Hadron Collider. These gamma photons would of course be absorbed by whatever is nearby, resulting in extreme heat and ultimately a thermal explosion with a power comparable to that of the Hiroshima bomb. Kaboom! But suppose we got this all wrong and there is no Hawking radiation; so once created, our 1 gram black hole is eternal. It would indeed fall through the floor and… well, not so much sink as fall freely towards the center of the Earth, interacting only infrequently with the atoms it runs across during its journey. Why? Because it would be insanely, insanely small. Something like 15 orders of magnitude smaller than a proton. And its supposedly enormous gravity? Not that enormous if you think about it unless you get very, very, very close. You’d have to be within less than one tenth of a micron from this black hole to experience 1 g acceleration. Would this 1 gram black hole accrete matter? Yes, it would. I calculated its so-called Bondi accretion rate assuming it’s sinking in a nonrelativistic medium with a density ten times that of water and a speed of sound of 1000 m/s, which is probably not a gross misrepresentation of the Earth’s interior. Long story short, assuming I used my calculator correctly, it would take roughly 10 billion times the present age of the universe… for the 1 g black hole to double in size and become a 2 g black hole.

If the “one-way” speed of light hasn’t yet been measured and we can just affirm the average 2-way speed of light for all points & perspectives is what measures c, what does that mean for ancient nighttime stars we see, that light’s not from long ago? Questions like this pop up regularly, and they are not silly. However, it is important to understand that ultimately, we do not measure speed, one-way, two-way or otherwise. We also do not measure distances. The only “pure” measurement that we can do without hidden assumptions is counting the ticks of a reliable clock. Of course even this measurement is based on an important assumption: Namely that in this universe, reliable clocks exist. Clocks that tick in sync; clocks that, when brought apart and later brought back together, will still continue to tick in sync (though they may have counted a different number of ticks in the meantime, while they were apart). All other measurements are derived from clock ticks. But… rulers! Oh, if idealized rulers existed… Well, then we wouldn’t have relativity theory, would we! An idealized ruler is perfectly rigid. Move one end and the other end moves instantaneously, no matter how far it is from the first! Spin the ruler at one end, and the other end will move around rapidly, perhaps many times faster than the vacuum speed of light! No such thing exists. Real rulers are physical objects, and when you move them around, different parts move at different speeds, depending on the material properties of the ruler, the speed of sound in that material and such things. In the end, the only way to properly calibrate a ruler is, you guessed it, by using a clever arrangement of reliable clocks and light signals. Yes, light signals. Because when two clocks are apart, we have no other means of relating their readings. So for instance, when we calibrate a ruler, we can attach a clock to one end, send a light signal to the other end and let it return, and then use the time elapsed on that clock to infer the length of the ruler. We can repeat this experiment using a clock on the other end, even a clock in the middle, but ultimately this is all we have: clocks and light signals. So we really have to turn things upside down. Forget about measuring the speed of light; assume that the vacuum speed of light is universal, then make a bunch of measurements, and check if the results are consistent with that assumption. They are. Of course you are free to propose alternatives. You are free to propose an alternative theory in which the speed of light is not constant, depends on direction, etc., and see if you can come up with results that are consistent with observation. However, unless your proposal is conceptually simpler than special relativity, do not be surprised if it is not received with enthusiasm. When two theories yield identical predictions, we generally prefer the one that’s simpler. And special relativity has a whole bunch of other factors supporting it, not the least the fact that Maxwell’s beautiful equations found a “native home” in four-dimensional spacetime, on account of the fact that the vacuum equations are conformally invariant in such a spacetime, and even in the presence of charges, the theory remains invariant under the Lorentz-Poincaré group. So for electromagnetism alone, special relativity is the native “playground”. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

If it turned out that white holes don't exist, how would it affect physics? It would confirm something that we think we already know, namely that this universe is reasonable well-behaved and causal. You see, a white hole is a time-reversed black hole. Take the “time reversed” bit seriously. A white hole isn’t a white hole because it repels things. Its gravity is just as attractive as a black hole’s gravity. (A time-reversed orbit is still an orbit, not a hyperbolic escape trajectory.) The reason why things can’t fall into the white hole is because they are not in the white hole in the future. (This is the time reversed version of a similar statement about black holes: Things can’t come out of black holes because they are not in the black hole in the past.) So if a white hole were to exist, it would mean that your own life is determined by your future: You can’t make the decision to fly into a white hole because you are not in the white hole in the future. Sounds illogical? Well, in a sense it is, if we think causality is logical. But white holes don’t care about causality. Their presence literally implies that the future determines the past. So be grateful perhaps that there are no white holes (as far as we know) in this universe. That means that our universe can behave, well, in a manner we consider “logical”, which is to say, causality applies and no effects precede their causes. Why would Americans rather drive their car for days than take the train? I live in Ottawa, Canada. I occasionally visit New York City. By car, a comfortable drive with the occasional rest stops takes about 8 hours and that includes crossing the border. It's 12:30 PM right now. If I were to hop into my car at 1 PM, chances are it'd still be daylight when I get out of my car somewhere in Manhattan. Now suppose I take the train. Google Maps tells me that I could depart tomorrow at 6:07 AM and arrive in Montreal at 8:11 AM. Three hours later, I would depart on Amtrak's Adirondack train, which could deliver me at Penn station a mere 11 hours later, at 10:15 PM. OK, how about return? Well, I could board the same Adirondack train the next day at 8:28 AM, heading back to Montreal. I'd arrive at Montreal's Gare Centrale at 8:16 PM. Too bad, that's after the last train that day left for Ottawa, so I'd have to get a hotel room and board the first train next morning at 6:20 AM. I'd arrive back at Ottawa's main railway station at 8:25 AM, just three minutes short of 24 hours since my departure at Penn Station. This does not include the time it takes to get to or from the railway station but it’s thankfully short, as I live not too far from Ottawa’s main railway station. OK, I could take a plane instead. The flight time from YOW to EWR (Newark) is only 90 minutes. Of course I need to be at the airport at least maybe 2 hours early, to go through customs preclearing. And then there is the ride to/from the airport. So I’d have to leave my home at least 3 hours prior to the scheduled departure, and it’d likely take at least an hour and a half to disembark, get my luggage, get a taxi and get from the airport to Manhattan. Overall? At least 6 hours travel time if everything goes according to plan. Granted, it's a little less than the road trip, but not that much less. And far less convenient. What about environmental costs? Google tells me that with Porter Airlines, one flight option only produces 55 kg of CO2 per passenger. But that's not much less* than the CO2 I'd produce burning up less than one full tank of fuel in my Honda Accord. This gets even more pronounced if I don’t travel alone: That 55 kg is per passenger, whereas my Honda’s fuel consumption would not change noticeably just because, say, my beautiful wife joins me for the trip. Would I like to take the train to NYC? Absolutely. And a century ago, I could have. The Ottawa & New York Railway ceased operations in 1957. I could not find a timetable but I doubt travel times were any worse than traveling with VIA Rail and Amtrak these days. Probably quicker and more comfortable, as a matter of fact. But those days are gone. What constitutes the "field" in quantum mechanics? Is it a vacuum devoid of anything, or is it composed of matter - the extension of matter (17)? None of the above. In physics (quantum or classical) a field is an entity that is a continuum: Something with a value at every point in space and every point in time. A field may have sources. Take, for instance, the magnetic field. Yes, “the” magnetic field, the one-and-only magnetic field that is present everywhere at all times. Its actual value depends on sources: namely, magnets! (Well, technically, moving charges, but I don’t want to get lost in the details). So if you hold a magnet in your hands, obviously near that magnet the magnetic field will be strong, as revealed, e.g., by the motion of an iron nail that you let lose in the magnet’s vicinity. But even very, very, very far from any magnet the magnetic field is still present; it’ll just be very weak. We can characterize the magnetic field by stating its value at every point in space and every moment in time. Of course that would be a tad inconvenient, so instead, we try to characterize the magnetic field wholesale, by writing down the equations that govern its behavior. If we have the right equations with the right boundary conditions, we can calculate the magnetic field at every point in space and at every point in time at the required precision. This works in both classical and quantum physics. The difference is in the nature of the field: In classical physics, strength (and direction, and perhaps other properties) of the field can be characterized by ordinary numbers, whereas in quantum physics, they are characterized by more complicated objects (Dirac called them q-numbers) which we can represent using matrices or using mathematical operators acting upon the famous wavefunction (which is really a mathematical entity that represents the overall state of the system.) Quantum physics, quantum field theory in particular, takes the concept of a field even more seriously though, because in quantum field theory, fields reign supreme. What we conceive as “particles” are really just properties of these fields, “excitations”. The neat thing about representing particles this way is that quantum field theory can account for the (observed) creation and annihilation of particles. Moreover, it is strictly causal: The theory is relativistic, and it does not allow any interaction that would be faster than light or backwards in time. So the next time you think about quantum electrodynamics, for instance, keep in mind that there are only two things in it: The one-and-only electromagnetic field (which consists of what we ordinarily think of as the electric and magnetic fields of Maxwell’s theory) and the one and only “electron field”, excitations of which are the charged electrons and their antiparticle counterparts, the positrons. Every electromagnetic phenomena: Light, radio waves, magnets, electrostatic attraction and repulsion, chemical bonds, etc., is ultimately the interplay between these two fields. Does the fact we cannot reconcile relativity or classical mechanics with quantum mechanics suggest we might never be capable of developing a theory of everything? If so, does that imply physics (and science) cannot fully explain the universe? What makes you think that we cannot reconcile classical mechanics with the quantum theory? It is reconciled just fine. The quantum theory builds upon classical mechanics (the Hamiltonian formalism). It refines it by recognizing, as valid states, states of a system that make no sense classically. However, classical mechanics re-emerges just fine in the limit of systems with a very large number of degrees of freedom or, alternatively, in the mathematical exercise of taking the Planck constant to zero. Special relativity is also doing perfectly fine with the quantum theory; quantum field theory, the foundational theory behind the Standard Model of particle physics, is fully relativistic. In fact, we can do quantum field theory even on the curved background of classical general relativity. Where things go awry is when we consider quantum matter as the source of classical gravitation. But here, an important statement is in order. It’s not that we don’t have perfectly sensible schemes to reconcile quantum matter and classical gravitation, either by quantizing gravitation or by taking the “semiclassical” approach of a hybrid theory. The fact that canonical quantization leads to a nonrenormalizable quantum theory of gravity is an issue but again, proposals abound as to how we might be able to overcome this obstacle. No, the real problem is not the lack of ideas. It’s the lack of data. Gravity is extremely, extremely weak. Direct detection of gravitons (assuming they exist) will likely never happen. Indirect detection of quantized effects of gravitation just might be possible, but I would not hold my breath. So here we are, without any real clues from Nature as to which direction to take. So it’s not so much that we cannot develop a theory of everything; rather, it’s that absent tangible clues, we simply don’t know which possible theory of everything to pick!

Why can't an observer just inside a supermassive black hole's event horizon escape if the gravity isn't strong enough at that point to tear him/her apart? First, allow me to challenge your premise. To “tear him apart”, you don’t just need gravity; you need tidal forces, which is to say, differences in gravity. Tides happen because for instance, different parts of the Earth are different distances away from the Moon, therefore lunar gravity acts on them with different strengths. Take this to the extreme, and in the vicinity of a small black hole or a neutron star, the differences become so large, your head and your big toe will want to follow wildly different orbits… thus you get torn apart. Never mind that, you are right, in the case of a very large supermassive black hole, this does not happen. In that case, tidal forces remain weak near the event horizon. But then, it’s not tidal forces that prevent you from escaping. It’s the sheer strength of gravity, not how it varies from point to point. We can measure the force of gravity, in principle, by calculating how powerful your rocket would need to be in order to simply hover. To escape, you obviously need a rocket even more powerful than that. And guess what… at the horizon, you’d need an infinitely powerful rocket simply to hover. Yet… inside the horizon it’s not even this that prevents you from escaping. What this has to do with is not so much the strength of gravity but the nature of that event horizon. You see, so long as you are outside the horizon, the horizon remains forever in the future. At the “present” of any outside observer, the horizon will not have formed yet, no matter how long they wait. The only way for any observer to make the horizon happen is by crossing it. Otherwise, it remains forever an unattainable future moment in time. But once you cross it, something else happens. Now the horizon is part of your past. I repeat, it’s not a place that you can return to. It does not have a shape. It’s a past moment in time. To return to it, to escape, you no longer need a rocket: you now need a time machine. Which, when you think about it, makes perfect sense even from the outside observers’ perspective. Recall I mentioned that for them, the horizon remains forever in the future. So if you were to escape from the black hole, to an outside observer it would imply that you are coming back from that future. There we go again… time machine. To sum up: at the horizon, you need an infinitely powerful rocket just to hover. Beyond the horizon (which is a future moment in time until/unless you cross it, when it becomes part of your past) you would need a time machine to escape.

According to relativity, gravity slows time (time dilation) and causes length contraction? Does Dark Energy, which is accelerating the expansion of the Universe, speed time and cause lengthening is space? OK, it doesn't exactly work that way. Gravity doesn't slow time, speed time, or change lengths. However, according to the theory of RELATIVITY (never forget the name!) observers in different gravitational fields will measure things differently. So what takes 1 second according to the clock of an observer in a strong gravitational field may take 2 seconds according to the clock of an observer in a weak gravitational field. This of course implies that we have a spatially varying gravitational field, which changes from point to point. Cosmological models are usually homogeneous models: that is, they assume that on average, the gravitational field is the same everywhere, it only changes with time. Over time it becomes weaker in an expanding cosmos, because matter flies apart and becomes less dense. When dark energy is present, stuff flies apart faster. And the rate at which it flies apart decreases more slowly. The Hubble parameter, rather than going down to zero as matter becomes less and less dense, settles down on a nonzero value instead. Expansion continues. As a result of that expansion, there is redshift. Some of it is just plain old velocity-related Doppler, due to things flying apart. But some of it (over cosmological scales, especially) is due to the time-varying gravitational field. On average, matter is less dense today than yesterday, so its overall gravity is weaker today than yesterday, so clocks today appear to tick faster than clocks yesterday. A signal emitted billions of years ago at a certain number of oscillations per second will show fewer oscillations per second as measured by a clock today. Dark energy does not fundamentally change this, but it alters the rate at which cosmological parameters, including the redshift, evolve over time. What if the singularity in the middle of a black hole was another black hole. As the mass squeezed down to a point going in then singularity goes to a black hole? OK, here is the problem: there is no singularity in the “middle” of a black hole. The singularity inside the event horizon of a Schwarzschild black hole is not some spot in the middle. As a matter of fact, the interior of the event horizon of a collapsing cloud of matter is well described by the same homogeneous and isotropic solution that describes an expanding or collapsing universe (see, e.g., Weinberg’s 1972 Gravitation and Cosmology, sec. 11.9). The singularity in this mini-universe is not a place; it is an inevitable future moment in time. So no, it’s not another black hole. It’s the “end of time”, end-of-the-world moment insofar as observers trapped inside the event horizon are concerned. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

How come vectors can have more than 3 elements? Shouldn't it only have 3 elements in Continuum Mechanics since it is a rank 1 tensor meaning it has 3 elements? I suspect that there is a deeper misunderstanding behind this question than the words reveal, and I sympathize. Back in my student days, I harbored similar misunderstandings that proved to be tough obstacles to overcome as I was trying to make sense of vectors, tensors and matrices. For what is a vector? As a good, mathematically gifted student I learned it early enough; It is either a pair or a triplet of numbers, a set of coordinates, really, usually written down in column form. So far, so good. What I knew worked just fine: I was able to do things like adding and subtracting vectors, calculating inner products and cross products, doing the usual things a high school student might be doing with vectors. I also knew about matrices. But apart from matrices specifically constructed to represent transformations, they had little to do with vectors. But then, I learned about tensors. Or rather, I was trying to. It's been pressed upon me that a tensor is different from a matrix. A matrix can be used to represent tensors, but the tensor's existence is not predicated on this representation. In fact, the same tensor can be represented differently using different coordinate systems. Now it took a while for this to sink in. Longer than I care to admit. Because eventually I had to discover something important: that the same thing is true for vectors and their representations as doublets or triplets of numbers! Unfortunately, we use the same word for both, so the distinction was not clear; whereas in the case of tensors, the words (tensor vs. matrix) differ, which was helpful. So if a vector is not a doublet or triplet of numbers, then what it? Why, it is an arrow, maybe: an arrow with a direction and a length. We can draw arrows without ever representing them as doublets or triplets of numbers. We can use geometry to find the arrow that is a sum of two arrows. Okay, so finally it was becoming (somewhat) clear: vectors and tensors are geometry, columns of numbers (really, 2x1 or 3x1 matrices) or matrices are their representations. But... I realized that I was still confused, because... Well, what about higher dimensions? Why, that's kind of easy: I can "imagine" arrows in four, five, or seventy-seven dimensions, and it makes sense that the corresponding representation would be a column of four, five or seventy-seven numbers. But it was still not good enough. For starters, I kept reading nonsense that, say, matrices form a "vector space". Say what? And then there's all this stuff in physics textbook about the "phase space" characterizing a system. And sometimes it has a lot of dimensions! What the... Back to the drawing board, I guess. And back I went, reading a bit more about abstract algebra. And that is when things finally became clear. What are the most general properties of vectors, really? Well, we add two vectors, we get a vector. So that's one. Another one is that we can make a vector smaller or larger by multiplying it by a number, and the result is still a vector. Hmmm. These are fundamental properties. In fact, a set with elements that can 1) be added together to form another element of the set, and 2) be multiplied by a real number to form another element of the set is a vector space. Anything that has these properties is a vector space. Numbers form a vector space. Columns of two numbers, columns of three (or four, or five, or seventy-seven) numbers form a vector space. Matrices? Well, I add to matrices together, I get a matrix. I multiply a matrix by a number, I get a matrix. Sure sounds like a vector space! And of course arrows form a vector space. Now I was getting somewhere! This abstract definition of a vector space seems to encompass everything we need to know about vector spaces! So confusingly, we call tensors of rank-1 "vectors", but tensors of any rank actually form a vector space. Sometimes, language can be misleading! Back to classical mechanics. Let's start with the simplest: a point particle in space. Indeed, its position is well represented by a three-dimensional vector, which can be represented, in turn, by a column of three numbers, the three coordinates. But wait: simply knowing where a particle is does not tell us where the particle will go next. For that, we also need the particle's velocity! Velocities in three-dimensional space can also be represented by three-dimensional vectors. So to fully describe the dynamics of our particle, we actually need two such vectors, i.e., six numbers! But this six-dimensional thing nonetheless behaves like a vector: we can add two of them together, and we can scale them by a factor. So there: the state of the particle "lives" as a vector in an abstract six-dimensional space! Now take something rigid that's not a particle but larger. That something has a position but also an orientation. And when we describe its motion, we need to know not only its velocity but also its rate of rotation. We are now up to 12 numbers, forming a vector space of 12 dimensions! Again, it is a vector space since position vectors, velocity vectors, rotation vectors, angular velocity vectors are all individually vector spaces, so when we lump them together, we get an entity that behaves like a vector. Perhaps you can see where this is taking us. Consider a system that's more complicated: say, it has several lose bits. Now we have even more "degrees of freedom". An in classical mechanics problems, each positional degree of freedom is accompanied by a corresponding velocity of some kind. Soon we have a lot of dimensions! Now, I stress, these multidimensional vectors are not arrows in space. they are not even columns of many numbers, though they can certainly be represented as such. They are abstract mathematical entities that satisfy the two criteria I outlined above: They can be added together and they can be scaled, and the result is a multidimensional vector of the same kind. As you mention, a vector really is a rank-1 tensor. But what, really, are tensors? Remember those inner products? We were taught in school that you form them by multiplying Cartesian vector components with each other and then summing the result. But this is not really the full picture. It's an oversimplification that is valid only in special cases. More generally, inner products are formed with the help of a rank-2 covariant tensor. If you want to think of it as a matrix product, think of that tensor as a matrix, and write the two vectors down, one as a row vector before the matrix, the other as a column vector after. Now multiply. If the matrix sandwiched between the two vectors is the identity matrix, the rules are the same as the inner product rules you learned in high school. But the matrix can be something else. (That matrix, or rather, the tensor it represents, will be the "metric".) So what do tensors do? Why, a rank-2 covariant tensor lets us form the inner products of two vectors. So a rank-3 tensor will help form an inner product of three vectors. And so on. Finally, tensors are making sense as well: they make a connection between vectors (which scale with a change of coordinates) and scalars (which don't care about coordinates) by basically compensating for any change of coordinates when the inner product is formed. So there, in a nutshell. Vectors as bunches of numbers as representations of vectors as arrows with lengths and directions, which really are a special case of things that can be added and scaled, which is the true definition of an abstract vector space; and the idea in classical mechanics that lumping together all positions and associated velocities for all the degrees of freedom of a system forms a vector, possibly with a large-ish number of dimensions. So what about continuous dynamics? That would be a system with an infinite number of degrees of freedom since, in principle, every bit of that system has its own position and velocity. True. But in this case, we can look at the equations that govern the system and realize soon enough that the properties of the system obey the same equations at all points. So no we have vector fields: the values change from position to position (or from abstract "position" to "position" in the phase space of classical mechanics) but the rules, the differential equations that govern them are the same. I know I didn't answer all questions. A short Quora answer is no substitute for a proper textbook. But I hope that at the very least, I offered enough to help make better sense of those textbooks. How do string theory and quantum theory explain light not being able to leave a black hole since light has no mass? Do we need relativity theory to explain this? Neither string theory nor the quantum theory are required for an explanation, and the fact that light has no rest mass (although it has energy-momentum, and is therefore subject to gravitation) is also irrelevant. What matters is that “to leave a black hole” you need to go back in time. Once “inside” the event horizon, that horizon is not a place that you can return to, but a past moment in time. For an observer outside the black hole, the event horizon remains forever in the future. For an observer who crosses the horizon, that event horizon becomes part of their past. So in both cases, “return” involves a) coming back from the far future (from the perspective of the outside observer) or b) going back to a past moment in time (from the perspective of the observer who crossed the horizon). In other words: time travel. You don’t need string theory or the quantum theory to explain why you cannot use a flashlight today to light up a scene yesterday. Not without a time machine anyway. The Schrödinger equation is deduced from the classical Hamiltonian: H = p 2 2 m + V ( q ) , by observing that we can substitute − i ℏ ∇ in place of p (and perhaps i ℏ ∂ t in place of H , and the equation remains valid, both sides now being operator-valued, acting on the function ψ = e i ( p q − H t ) / ℏ , and then turning the tables around and opting to solve for ψ instead: H ψ = − ℏ 2 2 m ∇ 2 ψ + V ( q ) ψ . Unfortunately this approach works only in the case of the nonrelativistic Hamiltonian. The relativistic equivalent would be the dispersion relation, which we could write as H 2 = p 2 + m 2 , but “quantizing” this will not produce meaningful results. The presence of second powers ultimately leads to an equation that predicts, e.g., negative probabilities in the Copenhagen interpretation. Dirac’s “magnificent trick” amounted to taking the “square root” of this equation in the form (I’m now using ℏ = 1 to keep things simple): H ψ = ( − i α ∇ + β m ) ψ . This approach will not work if α and β are numbers. But what if they are not? What if they obey a set of commutation relations like α i β + β α i = 0 , α i α j + α j α i = 0 , α 2 i = 1 ,    β 2 = 1. (NB: α is vector-valued, hence the indices.) There. This works if α i and β are constructed using the Dirac-matrices γ μ , and the function ψ on which they act is itself a four-component entity. Written in the usual relativistic form, then, we end up with i γ μ ∂ μ ψ − m ψ = 0. As it turns out, the four components of ψ can describe the two spin states of a fermion (like the electron) and the corresponding two spin states of its antiparticle. As I said, it is not so much a derivation but a deduction. It is mathematically consistent but that does not mean anything. What matters is that it is validated against reality: the equation accurately describes what we see in actual experiments. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

If you were sufficiently close to two colliding black holes, would distortions in space caused by the gravity waves be fatal (ignoring all of the other fatal phenomena like the accretion disk and tidal effects)? Well, technically yes, but by that time you are too close already and you’d be killed by those tides even in the absence of a collision and the resulting gravitational waves. [Pedantic note, with apologies: A “gravity wave” is what you see on the surface of the sea when it waves. A “gravitational wave” is a propagating change in the gravitational field away from sources.] The point is, gravitational waves are propagating changes. A single object produces a gravitational field that changes from place to place but it does not change over time in the inertial reference frame in which the object is at rest. But when we have two objects inspiraling towards each other, no such inertial frame exists. The gravitational field changes not just from place to place but also over time. These changes then ripple away towards infinity with ever decreasing amplitude, much like changes in the electromagnetic field do in response to electric charges undergoing accelerating motion. When the gravitational force changes from place to place, it represents a tidal force. Different parts of a body want to head in different directions or different rates. This can rip a body apart. There are tides near any gravitating object, and tides near a black hole can be very strong because we can get very close to a black hole (they are very compact). When the black holes inspiral, these tidal forces change. Those changes propagate. But they do not get stronger with distance, quite the contrary. And in the end, what kills us is not how the tidal forces change over time, but how strong they are in the first place. Get close enough to the black hole and you’ll find out! A little farther away, though… I once calculated that if you were about the same distance from the merger of two ~30 solar mass black holes as the Earth is from the Sun, you could actually hear the result as a loud rising then decaying sound. Yes, there can be sounds in space! Well, not exactly sounds as we know them, not a traveling longitudinal pressure wave in a medium, rather, transversal gravitational waves in the vacuum but in the end how they travel is not relevant; what is relevant is that at that distance, they are powerful enough to interact with our ears. If neutrinos always pass through everything, then how can it have any mass without interacting with the Higgs field? First of all, neutrinos do not always pass through everything; they almost always pass through almost everything, but that “almost” makes a lot of difference. This is why neutrinos are detectable. This is also why neutrinos, when they are present in insanely large numbers and encounter very dense stellar matter, contribute a great deal when, e.g., a supernova explosion unfolds. As to the origin of the neutrino mass, in our best models to date neutrinos are one of the exceptions: Their mass is not due to the Higgs mechanism. Neutrino mass is weird. For neutrinos, mass eigenstates (when the mass is a well-defined number) and flavor eigenstates (when the flavor, or type, of the neutrino is well-defined) do not coincide. Confining a neutrino’s flavor by measurement makes its mass indeterminate and vice versa. This is accounted for not by the Higgs mechanism, but by what is known as a “mass mixing matrix”, the so-called PMNS (Pontecorvo–Maki–Nakagawa–Sakata) matrix. The manner in which this matrix is introduced into the theory is independent of the Higgs field. In any case, this has nothing to do with the fact that neutrinos have no electric or color (strong force) charge, so they interact only through the “weak” interaction: an interaction that is just as strong at short range as electromagnetism, but mediated by very massive particles which means that the interaction is extremely short range, making it effectively weak (i.e., a neutrino very rarely gets close enough to another particle to be influenced by it).

Apparently as a mass approaches C, further acceleration requires exponentially greater energy. But, if any non-accelerating object can consider itself to be at rest, then why shouldn't any subsequent change to its velocity be as easy as at V=0? Oh, but it is just as easy. However, you must not forget how velocities are added in special relativity. So you have an object, happily traveling at… well, 0 m/s in its own reference frame. It’s a spacecraft. It turns on its rocket engine briefly and accelerates to 1 m/s relative to its earlier inertial reference frame. But this spacecraft was already traveling, say, at 299,792,450 m/s in your reference frame. Just 8 m/s short of the vacuum speed of light. And it turns on its rocket engine. So now you calculate its velocity in your own reference frame. Using, say, v 0 and Δ v for the initial velocity and the change in velocity, you use the relativistic velocity addition formula compute v = ( v 0 + Δ v ) / ( 1 + v 0 Δ v / c 2 ) and get… 299,792,450.00000005337 m/s. In other words, in your reference frame, the object’s velocity increased by just over 53 nanometers per second. For a more elaborate exposition of this problem, I recommend looking at one of the oldest Physics FAQ’s on the Interwebs, this description of The Relativistic Rocket.
